Holography for bulk-boundary local topological order
Corey Jones 1, Pieter Naaijkens 2, David Penneys 3

Abstract
. In our previous article [ arXiv: 2307.12552 ], we introduced local topological order (LTO) axioms for quantum spin systems which allowed us to define a physical boundary manifested by a net of boundary algebras in one dimension lower. This gives a formal setting for topological holography, where the braided tensor category of DHR bimodules of the physical boundary algebra captures the bulk topological order. In this article, we extend the LTO axioms to quantum spin systems equipped with a topological boundary, again producing a physical boundary algebra for the bulk-boundary system, whose category of (topological) boundary DHR bimodules recovers the topological boundary order. We perform this analysis in explicit detail for Levin-Wen and Walker-Wang bulk-boundary systems. Along the way, we introduce a 2D braided categorical net of algebras built from a unitary braided fusion category (UBFC). Such nets arise as boundary algebras of Walker-Wang models. We consider the canonical state on this braided categorical net corresponding to the standard topological boundary for the Walker-Wang model. Interestingly, in this state, the cone von Neumann algebras are type I with finite dimensional centers, in contrast with the type II and III cone von Neumann algebras from the Levin-Wen models studied in [ arXiv: 2307.12552 ]. Their superselection sectors recover the underlying unitary category of our UBFC, and we conjecture the superselection category also captures the fusion and braiding.



1.
Introduction

Topologically ordered spin systems are fundamental examples of quantum many-body systems whose ground states exhibit long-range entanglement.
A particularly interesting class of these systems exhibit
local topological order
(LTO), defined in terms of error correcting properties of their local ground state spaces.
This class includes all string net models
[
Kit97
,
Kit03
,
LW05
,
LLB21
]
, and thus the class of LTOs exhibits all possible non-chiral topological orders in (2+1)D.

In our previous work
[
JNPW23
]
, we introduced additional LTO-type axioms which allow for a well-defined notion of the
physical boundary
for an LTO system in terms of a
boundary algebra
.
The physical boundary is obtained by cutting the system using a hyperplane.
The boundary algebra has the structure of a net of
\rm{C}^{*}
-algebras in one dimension lower than the original LTO system.
The boundary algebra allows for a parameterization of boundary states of system, and in (2+1)D it captures the bulk topological order via
DHR bimodules

[
Jon24
]
, manifesting a kind of topological holographic principle in the spirit of
[
CW23
,
IW23
]
.

In this article, we extend this story to the case of
topological boundaries
of locally topologically ordered spin systems in 2+1 and 3+1 dimensions, introducing the notion of
boundary LTO
.
The topological boundary comes from a boundary of the underlying (bulk) lattice on which the system is defined.
Boundary LTOs are designed to capture the standard topological boundaries of string-net models.
We construct a (physical) boundary algebra for the topological bulk-boundary system described by a boundary LTO, and define a boundary DHR category
\text{DHR}^{\partial}
meant to capture the structure of topological boundary excitations and their relation to the bulk.

Our first examples are 1D topological boundaries for 2D Levin-Wen models associated to a unitary fusion category (UFC)
{\mathcal{C}}
and a unitary module category
{\mathcal{M}}
(pictured left below)
[
KK12
]
.
Our second family of main examples are 2D topological boundaries for the 3D Walker-Wang model associated to a unitary braided fusion category (UBFC)
{\mathcal{A}}
and a unitary
{\mathcal{A}}
-enriched UFC
{\mathcal{X}}

[
HBJP23
,
GHK+24
]
(pictured right below).
In the pictures below,
red denotes the bulk, black denotes the topological boundary, and the cut corresponding to the physical boundary is denoted in blue.

\scriptstyle{\mathcal{K}}

\scriptstyle{\mathcal{K}}

Our first result analyzes the boundary LTOs of Levin-Wen models.
For a Levin-Wen model built from a string-net for some UFC
{\mathcal{C}}
, we study the case of standard boundaries given microsopically by a
{\mathcal{C}}
-module category
{\mathcal{M}}_{\mathcal{C}}
.
In this case, the boundary algebras associated to the bulk system are fusion spin chains, and the boundary algebras associated to the bulk-boundary system are natural ‘finite index’ (in the sense of
[
Jon83
]
) extensions of half-infinite fusion spin chains called
fusion module spin chains
, which are precisely the setting of classical subfactor theory
[
JS97
,
EK98
]
(see also
[
CHPS21
]
for how these fusion module algebras arise).
We may thus apply extant operator algebraic machinery to deduce that the boundary DHR category is the dual category
\End({\mathcal{M}}_{\mathcal{C}})
as expected.

To state the following theorem, let
{\mathcal{C}}
be a UFC and
{\mathcal{M}}_{\mathcal{C}}
an indecomposable module category.
We have a natural boundary LTO on the 2D square lattice whose bulk LTO is a version of the Levin-Wen model studied in
[
LW05
]
, and whose boundary projections are defined in terms of
{\mathcal{M}}
as in
[
KK12
]
.
We denote the (physical) boundary algebra of this bulk-boundary system by
{\mathfrak{M}}
.
Using standard subfactor techniques (which we summarize in Appendix
A
), we demonstrate the following.

Theorem A
.

The Levin-Wen bulk-boundary system is a boundary LTO.
The boundary algebra
\mathfrak{M}
is a fusion module spin chain, and its boundary DHR bimodules are given by the UFC
\mathsf{DHR}^{\partial}(\mathfrak{M})\cong\End({\mathcal{M}}_{\mathcal{C}})
.

Our next main topic is the analysis of Walker-Wang LTOs and their boundary LTOs.
Associated to a unitary
braided
fusion category (UBFC)
{\mathcal{B}}
, the Walker-Wang model is a (3+1)D string-net model which are easily seen to satisfy the LTO axioms (see Theorem
5.6
).
The boundary algebra for the
{\mathcal{B}}
Walker-Wang model can naturally be identified with a two-dimensional version of a fusion spin chain which we call a
braided categorical net
.
The input for this construction is a UBFC
{\mathcal{B}}
and a (strong) tensor generating object
X\in\mathcal{B}
; for Walker-Wang models,
X
is the sum over simples.

Braided categorical nets are interesting mathematical objects in their own right.
For example, when a braided categorical net is built from a Drinfeld center
Z({\mathcal{C}})
, the net of algebras is
bounded spread isomorphic
to the net of local operators in the ‘flux sector’ of a Levin-Wen model
[
KJS+24
]
(see also §
4.2
below), which is purely 2D.
Transporting the ground state of Levin-Wen across this isomorphism yields an interesting topological boundary state on the
Z({\mathcal{C}})
braided categorial net, which is generalizable to arbitrary UBFCs
\mathcal{B}
.
This gives a new example of a
duality
for 2D abstract quantum spin systems
[
JSW24
,
Eck25
]
.
The following theorem is interesting in comparison with the nets of type
\rm II
and type
\rm III
cone von Neumann algebras from Levin-Wen models from
[
JNPW23
]
.

Theorem B
.

The cone von Neumann algebras of the
{\mathcal{B}}
braided categorical net in this topological boundary state are type
{\mathrm{I}}
von Neumann algebras with finite dimensional centers.

These braided categorical nets with their natural states described above give the first examples to our knowledge of nets of type
{\mathrm{I}}
von Neumann algebras with interesting superselection theory in the sense of
[
Naa11
,
Naa17
,
Oga22
]
; the extension of superselection theory to the non-factorial setting appears in
[
BBC+24
]
.

Theorem C
.

The
{\mathrm{W}}^{*}
-category

Returning to our main line of investigation, the universailty classes of topological boundaries of
\mathcal{B}
Walker-Wang models correspond to
\mathcal{B}
-enriched fusion categories
[
HBJP23
]
, i.e., a UFC
{\mathcal{X}}
equipped with a braided central functor from
\mathcal{B}
to
Z({\mathcal{X}})

[
KZ18a
,
HPT16
,
MP19
]
.
Microscopic models for these boundaries were introduced in
[
HBJP23
,
GHK+24
]
.
We show that these bulk-boundary models are boundary LTOs, and that their physical boundary algebras assemble into a braided categorical net
{\mathfrak{X}}
.

Theorem D
.

The Walker-Wang bulk-boundary system for
{\mathcal{B}}\to Z({\mathcal{X}})
is a boundary LTO.
The boundary algebra
{\mathfrak{X}}
is a braided categorical net, and
its category of boundary DHR bimodules
\mathsf{DHR}^{\partial}(\mathfrak{X})
is unitarily braided equivalent to the
enriched center

Z^{\mathcal{B}}({\mathcal{X}})
, the Müger centralizer of
{\mathcal{B}}
in
Z({\mathcal{X}})
.

Our analysis is performed using the folding trick, leading to a new inclusion of von Neumann algebras which could reasonably be called the
enriched symmetric enveloping algebra
of an ‘enriched subfactor’ in the spirit of
[
Pop94
]
.
As a corollary, we also obtain a characterization of the
bulk
DHR bimodules for Walker-Wang models.

Theorem E
.

The
{\mathcal{B}}
Walker-Wang model is an LTO, and the DHR category
\mathsf{DHR}({\mathfrak{B}})
of its boundary algebra
{\mathfrak{B}}
is unitarily braided equivalent to
Z_{2}({\mathcal{B}})
, the Müger center of
{\mathcal{B}}
.

The main application of DHR bimodules for boundary algebras for LTOs in 2D is to give a model independent way to recover the bulk topological order.
We again find that the boundary DHR bimodules for the
{\mathcal{X}}
topological boundary for the
{\mathcal{B}}
Walker-Wang model
recover the topological boundary excitations.
However, for the (3+1)D
{\mathcal{B}}
Walker-Wang model alone, the DHR bimodules fall short in this regard.
Indeed, the topological order of a (3+1)D system is a braided fusion 2-category, whereas the DHR bimodules merely form a braided (and in (3+1)D,
symmetric
) fusion category.
Indeed, our bulk DHR only recovers information concerning
point defects
of the underlying topological quantum field theory, missing the line defects.
However, if we truncate the boundary algebra to obtain a bulk-boundary system for a fusion spin chain, our result says the category of boundary DHR bimodules is
{\mathcal{B}}
as a braided fusion category.
From this, we can take
Z(\mathsf{Mod}({\mathcal{B}}))
to again describe the entire bulk topological order.
However, this description is somewhat unsatisfactory, and it would be desirable to extend the notion of DHR bimodule to directly construct the braided fusion 2-category of all low energy excitations.

We recall the basic setting and main results of
[
JNPW23
]
in §
2
, before we introduce the notion of boundary LTO and the category of boundary DHR bimodules.
These notions are analyzed in §
3.1
for the Levin-Wen model with gapped boundary.
Braided categorical nets are defined (and their superselection sectors identified) in §
4
.
Finally, we consider the (3+1)D Walker-Wang model in §
5
and identify its boundary algebras and corresponding (boundary) DHR bimodules.
Some useful techniques from subfactor theory are collected in Appendix
A
.

2.
Background

2.1.
Nets of algebras and local topological order axioms

We consider
abstract quantum spin systems
given by a (local) net of algebras defined on some discrete set
{\mathcal{L}}
.
In our applications, typically
{\mathcal{L}}={\mathbb{Z}}^{d}
.

Definition 2.1

(Net of algebras)
.

Let
{\mathcal{L}}
be a discrete set and
{\mathfrak{A}}
a unital
{\mathrm{C}}^{*}
-algebra.
A
net of algebras
is a mapping which assigns a unital
{\mathrm{C}}^{*}
-subalgebra
{\mathfrak{A}}(\Lambda)\subset{\mathfrak{A}}
to each finite subset
2
2

2

It is enough to only specify
{\mathfrak{A}}(\Lambda)
for “nice” regions
\Lambda
, e.g. all rectangles.

\Lambda\subset{\mathcal{L}}
such that

(1)

{\mathfrak{A}}(\emptyset)={\mathbb{C}}1_{\mathfrak{A}}
;

(2)

(Isotony)
{\mathfrak{A}}(\Lambda)\subset{\mathfrak{A}}(\Delta)
if
\Lambda\subset\Delta
;

(3)

(Locality)
[{\mathfrak{A}}(\Lambda),{\mathfrak{A}}(\Delta)]=0
if
\Lambda\cap\Delta=\emptyset
;

(4)

(Quasi-locality/density)
\bigcup_{\Lambda}{\mathfrak{A}}(\Lambda)
is norm-dense in
{\mathfrak{A}}
.

We will also refer to
{\mathfrak{A}}
as the
quasi-local algebra
.
Physically, it describes those operators that can be approximated arbitrarily well (in norm) by strictly local operators.
For any (not-necessarily finite)
\Lambda\subset{\mathcal{L}}
we can define
{\mathfrak{A}}(\Lambda)
as the norm-closure of
\bigcup_{\Delta\subset\Lambda}{\mathfrak{A}}(\Lambda)
, where the union is over all finite subsets contained in
\Lambda
.
Note that
{\mathfrak{A}}({\mathcal{L}})={\mathfrak{A}}
.

For a net of algebras
{\mathfrak{A}}
on a
{\mathbb{Z}}^{d}
lattice, a net of projections is an assignment of a projection
p_{\Lambda}\in{\mathfrak{A}}(\Lambda)
for every bounded rectangle
\Lambda
.
We furthermore demand that
\Lambda\mapsto p_{\Lambda}
is ordered by reverse inclusion, i.e.
p_{\Delta}\leq p_{\Lambda}
if
\Lambda\subset\Delta
.
In our examples there always is a natural translation symmetry on
{\mathcal{L}}
, inducing a translation symmetry
\tau_{x}({\mathfrak{A}}(\Lambda))={\mathfrak{A}}(\Lambda+x)
on
{\mathfrak{A}}
, and we will assume that
p_{\Lambda}
is translation invariant.

We say a rectangle
\Lambda
is

•

completely surrounded
by another rectange
\Delta
by
surrounding constant

s>0
, denoted
\Lambda\ll_{s}\Delta
, if
\Lambda\subset\Delta
, and the
\ell^{\infty}
ball of radius
s
about every vertex
v\in\Lambda
(a rectangle centered at
v
with side lengths
2s
) fits inside
\Delta
,
and

•

surrounded
by another rectange
\Delta
by
surrounding constant

s>0
, denoted
\Lambda\Subset_{s}\Delta

if
\Lambda\subset\Delta
, the intersection
\partial\Lambda\cap\partial\Delta
occurs in a hyperplane of codimension one along a standard axis in our
{\mathbb{Z}}^{d}
lattice, and for all other points
v\in\Delta\setminus\Lambda
, an
\ell^{\infty}
ball of radius
s
containing
v
fits inside
\Delta
.

\Delta
\Lambda
\Lambda\ll_{s}\Delta

\Delta
\Lambda
\Lambda\Subset_{s}\Delta

Given
\Lambda\Subset_{s}\Delta
, we define a unital
*
-algebra of ‘boundary error operators’ by

{\mathfrak{B}}(\Lambda\Subset_{s}\Delta):=\left\{xp_{\Delta}\middle|x\in p_{\Lambda}{\mathfrak{A}}(\Lambda)p_{\Lambda}\text{ and }xp_{\Delta^{\prime}}=p_{\Delta^{\prime}}x\text{ whenever }\Lambda\Subset_{s}\Delta^{\prime}\text{ with }\partial\Lambda\cap\partial\Delta^{\prime}=\partial\Lambda\cap\partial\Delta\right\}.

The local topological order axioms
[
JNPW23
]
for a net of algebras
{\mathfrak{A}}
equipped with a net of projections
(p_{\Lambda})
are as follows.
There is a ‘sufficient largeness’ constant
r>0
and a
‘surrounding constant’
s>0
such that

(LTO1)

Whenever
\Lambda\ll_{s}\Delta
,
p_{\Delta}{\mathfrak{A}}(\Lambda)p_{\Delta}={\mathbb{C}}p_{\Delta}
.

(LTO2)

Whenever
\Lambda\Subset_{s}\Delta
,
p_{\Delta}{\mathfrak{A}}(\Lambda)p_{\Delta}={\mathfrak{B}}(\Lambda\Subset_{s}\Delta)p_{\Delta}
.

(LTO3)

Whenever

\Lambda_{1}\subset\Lambda_{2}\Subset_{s}\Delta
with

\partial\Lambda_{1}\cap\partial\Delta=\partial\Lambda_{2}\cap\partial\Delta
,

{\mathfrak{B}}(\Lambda_{1}\Subset_{s}\Delta)={\mathfrak{B}}(\Lambda_{2}\Subset_{s}\Delta)
.

(LTO4)

Whenever
\Lambda\Subset_{s}\Delta_{1}\subset\Delta_{2}
with

\partial\Lambda\cap\partial\Delta_{1}=\partial\Lambda\cap\partial\Delta_{2}
,
the map
x\mapsto xp_{\Delta_{2}}
is injective.

Axioms
(LTO3)
and
(LTO4)
ensure that the boundary error operators
{\mathfrak{B}}(\Lambda\Subset_{s}\Delta)
only depend on the intersection
\partial\Lambda\cap\partial\Delta
and not on the choices of
\Lambda,\Delta
beyond them being sufficiently large with
\Lambda\Subset_{s}\Delta
.

We can think of our axioms in terms of error correcting codes.
The first axiom is related to the LTQO conditions
[
BHM10
,
BH11
]
and implies that for tensor product nets of algebras, the projections associated to sufficiently large rectangles project onto a code space that corrects against errors localized
away
from the boundary of the rectangle.
The second axioms ensures all localized errors whose supports only meet the boundary in a small region are correctable to errors localized near where the support meets the boundary.
The algebras
{\mathfrak{B}}(\Lambda\Subset_{s}\Delta)
collect these local error operators into a net of algebras on a rectangle lattice one dimension smaller, as we recall below.
The other two axioms ensure that the resulting nets have nice properties (e.g., being local in a suitable sense), which we will explain below.
The operators in
{\mathfrak{B}}(\Lambda\Subset_{s}\Delta)
are related to the ‘patch operators’ in
[
CW23
,
IW23
]
and our motivation to study them is the same, namely the holographic bulk-boundary duality.

Example 2.2
.

Kitaev’s Toric Code
[
Kit97
]
was shown to satisfy
(LTO1)
–
(LTO4)
in
[
JNPW23
, §3]
.

Example 2.3
.

Kitaev’s Quantum Double model
[
Kit03
]
was shown to satisfy
(LTO1)
–
(LTO4)
in
[
CHK+24
, §III]
.

Example 2.4
.

The unitary tensor category version of the Levin-Wen model from
[
Kon14
,
GHK+24
]

was shown to satisfy
(LTO1)
–
(LTO4)
in
[
JNPW23
, §4]
.

2.2.
The canonical state and the net of boundary error operators

By
(LTO1)
, we get a canonical state
\psi
on the quasi-local algebra
{\mathfrak{A}}
determined by taking norm limits under the formula

p_{\Delta}xp_{\Delta}=\psi(x)p_{\Delta}\qquad\qquad\qquad x\in{\mathfrak{A}}(\Lambda)\text{ and }\Lambda\ll_{s}\Delta.

It was shown in
[
JNPW23
, Cor. 2.24]
that if
\Delta\mapsto p_{\Delta}
is translation invariant,
\psi
is the unique translation invariant state satisfying
\psi(p_{\Lambda})=1
for all
\Lambda
, and thus
\psi
is pure.

Now given a choice of codimension 1 sub-lattice
{\mathcal{K}}\subset{\mathcal{L}}
and a distinguished choice of half-space
{\mathbb{H}}
of
{\mathcal{L}}
to one side of
{\mathcal{K}}
, the axioms
(LTO1)
–
(LTO4)
construct a net of algebras
{\mathfrak{B}}
on
{\mathcal{K}}
called the
boundary algebra
together with a quantum channel
{\mathbb{E}}:{\mathfrak{A}}_{{\mathbb{H}}}\to{\mathfrak{B}}
.

The main idea is that given
\Lambda\Subset_{s}\Delta\subset{\mathbb{H}}
with
s
sufficiently large
and
I:=\partial\Lambda\cap\partial\Delta\subset{\mathcal{K}}
,
the algebra

{\mathfrak{B}}(\Lambda\Subset_{s}\Delta)

only depends on the boundary rectangle
I
and sites nearby in
\Lambda
, not the specific choices of
\Lambda
and
\Delta
.
Indeed, choosing
\Lambda_{I}\subset\Lambda
to be the smallest sufficiently large rectangle with
\partial\Lambda_{I}\cap{\mathcal{K}}=I

and
\Delta_{I}\subset\Delta
to be the smallest rectangle with
\Lambda_{I}\Subset_{s}\Delta_{I}
with
\partial\Lambda_{I}\cap\partial\Delta_{I}=I
,
we define the
boundary algebra

{\mathfrak{B}}(I):={\mathfrak{B}}(\Lambda_{I}\Subset_{s}\Delta_{I}).

It was shown in
[
JNPW23
, Construction 2.28]
that
I\mapsto{\mathfrak{B}}(I)
defines a net of algebras on
{\mathcal{K}}
.

We now observe that we get a quantum channel
{\mathbb{E}}
from

{\mathfrak{A}}_{\mathbb{H}}:=\varinjlim_{\Lambda\subset{\mathbb{H}}}{\mathfrak{A}}(\Lambda)

to
{\mathfrak{B}}=\varinjlim{\mathfrak{B}}(I)

by taking norm limits under the formula

p_{\Delta}xp_{\Delta}={\mathbb{E}}(x)p_{\Delta}\qquad\qquad\qquad x\in{\mathfrak{A}}(\Lambda),\,\,\Lambda\Subset_{s}\Delta\subset{\mathbb{H}},\text{ and }\partial\Lambda\cap\partial\Delta\subset{\mathcal{K}}.

Moreover, for any
x\in{\mathfrak{A}}_{{\mathbb{H}}}
supported sufficiently far away from
{\mathcal{K}}
,
{\mathbb{E}}_{\mathbb{H}}(x)=\psi(x)
.
We thus get a
state-based approach
to boundary theories, where any state
\phi
on
{\mathfrak{B}}
can be uniquely extended to
{\mathfrak{A}}_{\mathbb{H}}
by
\phi\circ{\mathbb{E}}
, and
\phi\circ{\mathbb{E}}
will still restrict to
\psi
sufficiently far away from
{\mathcal{K}}
.

Example 2.5
.

In
[
JNPW23
, Thm. 4.8 and Rem. 4.9]
, it was shown that the boundary algebra for the unitary tensor category version of the Levin-Wen model from
[
Kon14
,
GHK+24
]

is a
fusion spin chain
.

In more detail, consider a unitary fusion category (UFC)
{\mathcal{C}}
equipped with a
strong tensor generator

X
, meaning that there exists an
n
such that every simple object in
{\mathcal{C}}
is isomorphic to a summand of
X^{\otimes n}
.
For a finite interval
I\subset{\mathbb{Z}}
, we define the finite dimensional
{\mathrm{C}}^{*}
-algebra
{\mathfrak{F}}(I):=\End_{\mathcal{C}}(X^{\otimes|I|})
.
If
I\subset J
there is an obvious inclusion of the corresponding algebras, by tensoring with copies of
\id_{X}
.
Note that this is compatible with the ‘geometric’ locality of
{\mathbb{Z}}
, and hence we get a net of algebras
{\mathfrak{F}}
called the
fusion spin chain
associated to
({\mathcal{C}},X)
.

One can then build a Levin-Wen model on a
{\mathbb{Z}}^{2}
lattice where the local Hilbert spaces are given by

{\mathcal{C}}(X\otimes X\to X\otimes X)

equipped with the GNS inner product from the categorical trace.
The boundary algebra along a 1D hyperplane will then be bounded spread isomorphic to the fusion spin chain
{\mathfrak{F}}
using a skein module argument as in
[
JNPW23
, Thm. 4.8]
.
Indeed, by semisimplicity, whenever
|I|\geq n
,
{\mathfrak{B}}(I)={\mathfrak{F}}(I)
by the following essential lemma.

Lemma 2.6

(Semisimple commutation)
.

Suppose
{\mathcal{C}}
is a semisimple category and
X\in{\mathcal{C}}
such that
{\mathcal{C}}(c\to X)\neq 0
for all
c\in\Irr({\mathcal{C}})
.
Then for any
a\in{\mathcal{C}}
, the commutant of the left action of
\End_{\mathcal{C}}(X)
on
{\mathcal{C}}(a\to X)
by postcomposition is the right action of
\End_{\mathcal{C}}(a)
by pre-composition.

Proof.

By semisimplicity, we can write

{\mathcal{C}}(a\to X)=\bigoplus_{c\in\Irr({\mathcal{C}})}{\mathcal{C}}(a\to c)\otimes{\mathcal{C}}(c\to X).

Observe that
{\mathcal{C}}(c\to X)
is an irreducible
\End_{\mathcal{C}}(X)
-module for each
c\in\Irr({\mathcal{C}})
, and
{\mathcal{C}}(a\to c)
then acts as a multiplicity space.
We then see that

\displaystyle\End_{\End_{\mathcal{C}}(X)}({\mathcal{C}}(a\to X))

\displaystyle=\bigoplus_{c\in\Irr({\mathcal{C}})}\End({\mathcal{C}}(a\to c))=\bigoplus_{c\in\Irr({\mathcal{C}})}{\mathcal{C}}(a\to c)\otimes\underbrace{{\mathcal{C}}(a\to c)^{\vee}}_{\cong{\mathcal{C}}(c\to a)}

\displaystyle=\bigoplus_{c\in\Irr({\mathcal{C}})}{\mathcal{C}}(a\to c)\otimes{\mathcal{C}}(c\to a)=\End_{\mathcal{C}}(a).\qed

2.3.
DHR bimodules

DHR bimodules where introduced in
[
Jon24
]
as an analog of the DHR superselection theory
[
Haa96
]
for abstract spin systems.
In
[
JNPW23
]
it was shown that the DHR bimodules of a ‘boundary net’ can be thought of as being holographically dual to the bulk topological order in Levin-Wen models or the toric code.
We recall the main ideas here, giving a fairly complete sketch of the main argument.

In this section,
A,B
will denote unital
{\mathrm{C}}^{*}
-algebras.

Definition 2.7
.

A right Hilbert
{\mathrm{C}}^{*}

B
-module
Y_{B}
is a right
B
-module equipped with a right
B
-valued inner product.
Moreover, we require that
Y
is complete with respect to the norm
\|\xi\|:=\|\langle\xi|\xi\rangle_{B}\|_{B}^{1/2}
.

A bounded operator
T:Y_{B}\to Y_{B}
is called
adjointable
if there is another operator
T^{\dagger}:Y_{B}\to Y_{B}
called the
adjoint
such that

\langle\eta|T\xi\rangle_{B}=\langle T^{\dagger}\eta|\xi\rangle_{B}
for all
\eta,\xi\in Y
.
Adjoints are unique when they exist, and they are automatically bounded by the Closed Graph Theorem.
We denote the space of adjointable operators by
\End(Y_{B})
, which is again a
{\mathrm{C}}^{*}
-algebra.

A Hilbert
{\mathrm{C}}^{*}

A-B
bimodule (sometimes called a
correspondence
) is a right Hilbert module
Y_{B}
together with a left
A
-action by adjointable operators.
We denote the category of
A-B
bimodules by
\mathsf{Bim}(A,B)
.
We refer the reader to
[
BLM04
, §8]
(see also
[
Pas73
,
Rie74
]
and
[
CHPJP22
, §2]
) for the definition of the Connes fusion relative tensor product for bimodules, which we will denote by
\boxtimes
, and further details.
This makes
\mathsf{Bim}(A)
into a
\rm{C}^{*}
tensor category.

Definition 2.8
.

Suppose
Y_{B}
is a right Hilbert
B
-module.
Each
\eta\in Y
gives a right
B
-linear creation operator
L_{\eta}:B\to Y
given by
b\mapsto\eta b
, which is adjointable with
L_{\eta}^{\dagger}\xi=\langle\eta|\xi\rangle_{B}
.

A right Hilbert
B
-module
Y_{B}
is called
finitely generated projective (fgp)
if there is a finite set
\{\beta_{i}\}_{i=1}^{n}\subset Y
called a
Y_{B}
-
basis
such that
\sum_{i}L_{\beta_{i}}L_{\beta_{i}}^{\dagger}=1
.
Such a
Y_{B}
-basis gives an explicit isomorphism
Y_{B}\cong pB^{n}_{B}
where

p\in M_{n}(B)
is the orthogonal projection whose entries are given by

p_{ij}:=\langle\beta_{i}|\beta_{j}\rangle_{B}.

Moreover, if
{}_{A}Y_{B}
carries a left
A
-action by adjointable operators, the corresponding left
A
-action on
B^{n}
given by

(a\cdot(b_{j}))_{i}:=\sum_{j}\langle\beta_{i}|a\beta_{j}\rangle_{B}b_{j}

promotes the above right
B
-module isomorphism to an
A-B
bimodule isomorphism.

Definition 2.9
.

Suppose
{\mathfrak{A}}
is a net of algebras on a lattice
{\mathcal{L}}
and
{}_{\mathfrak{A}}Y_{\mathfrak{A}}\in\mathsf{Bim}({\mathfrak{A}})
.
We say that a vector
\xi\in Y
is
localized
in a rectangle
\Lambda
if

a\xi=\xi a\qquad\qquad\qquad\forall\,a\in{\mathfrak{A}}(\Delta),\quad\forall\,\Delta\subset\Lambda^{c}.

Recall that if
B\subset A
is a unital inclusion of
{\mathrm{C}}^{*}
-algebras, the
centralizer
of
B\subset A
is

Z_{A}(B):=\left\{a\in A\middle|ab=ba\text{ for all }b\in B\right\}.

Lemma 2.10
.

If
\eta,\xi\in Y\in\mathsf{Bim}({\mathfrak{A}})
are both localized in
\Lambda
and
a\in{\mathfrak{A}}(\Lambda)
, then

\langle\eta|a\xi\rangle_{{\mathfrak{A}}}\in Z_{{\mathfrak{A}}}({\mathfrak{A}}(\Delta))
for all
\Delta\subset\Lambda^{c}
.

Proof.

For all
x\in{\mathfrak{A}}(\Delta)
,

x\langle\eta|a\xi\rangle_{{\mathfrak{A}}}=\langle\eta x^{*}|a\xi\rangle_{{\mathfrak{A}}}=\langle x^{*}\eta|a\xi\rangle_{{\mathfrak{A}}}=\langle\eta|xa\xi\rangle_{{\mathfrak{A}}}=\langle\eta|a\xi x\rangle_{{\mathfrak{A}}}=\langle\eta|a\xi\rangle_{{\mathfrak{A}}}x
.
∎

If we know our net of algebras satisfies algebraic Haag duality (see the next definition), the above lemma allows us to conclude that
\langle\eta|\xi\rangle_{{\mathfrak{A}}}
actually lies in the algebra
{\mathfrak{A}}(\Lambda)
.

Definition 2.11

(
[
Jon24
]
)
.

A net of algebras
{\mathfrak{A}}
satisfies
algebraic Haag duality

if for every rectangle
\Lambda
,

Z_{{\mathfrak{A}}}({\mathfrak{A}}(\Lambda^{c}))={\mathfrak{A}}(\Lambda)
, where
{\mathfrak{A}}(\Lambda^{c})\subset{\mathfrak{A}}
is the
{\mathrm{C}}^{*}
-algebra generated by all the
{\mathfrak{A}}(\Delta)
such that
\Delta\subset\Lambda^{c}
.

Definition 2.12

(
[
Jon24
]
)
.

Suppose
{\mathfrak{A}}
is a net of algebras on our lattice
{\mathcal{L}}

and
{}_{\mathfrak{A}}Y_{\mathfrak{A}}\in\mathsf{Bim}({\mathfrak{A}})
is fgp.
For a rectangle
\Lambda\subset{\mathcal{L}}
, we say that
{}_{\mathfrak{A}}Y_{\mathfrak{A}}
is
localizable in
\Lambda

if there is a
Y_{\mathfrak{A}}
basis localized in
\Lambda
.

We say
{}_{\mathfrak{A}}Y_{\mathfrak{A}}
is
localizable
or a
DHR bimodule
if for any
\Lambda
sufficiently large,
{}_{\mathfrak{A}}Y_{\mathfrak{A}}
is localizable in
\Lambda
.
Observe that DHR bimodules are closed under composition of bimodules, and thus form a full
{\mathrm{C}}^{*}
tensor subcategory of
\mathsf{Bim}({\mathfrak{A}})
, denoted
\mathsf{DHR}({\mathfrak{A}})
.

One uses this localizability of DHR bimodules to define a unitary braiding for
\mathsf{DHR}({\mathfrak{A}})
similar to the strategy in
[
CJP24
]
.

Definition 2.13
.

Suppose that
{\mathfrak{A}}
satisfies algebraic Haag duality.
Suppose
Y,Z\in\mathsf{DHR}({\mathfrak{A}})
.
Choose projective bases
\{b_{i}\},\{c_{j}\}
for
Y,Z
respectively which are localized in sufficiently large rectangles
\Lambda,\Delta
which are sufficiently far apart in
{\mathcal{L}}
(see
[
Jon24
]
for the precise details).
We define

u^{\Lambda,\Delta}_{Y,Z}:Y\boxtimes_{\mathfrak{A}}Z\rightarrow Z\boxtimes_{\mathfrak{A}}Y\qquad\qquad\text{by}\qquad\qquad\sum_{i,j}b_{i}\boxtimes c_{j}a_{ij}\mapsto\sum_{i,j}c_{j}\boxtimes b_{i}a_{ij}.

One verifies this formula is a well-defined unitary
{\mathfrak{A}}-{\mathfrak{A}}
bimodule map which is independent of the choices of
\Lambda,\Delta
(provided they are sufficiently large and separated), and also independent of the choices of projective bases.
(When our lattice
{\mathcal{L}}
is 1-dimensional, we must require that our two rectangles are always linearly ordered in the same way, or we may accidentally get the reverse braiding.)

To calculate
\mathsf{DHR}({\mathfrak{A}})
and its braiding in practice, we may use the following equivalent characterization of a DHR bimodule (for similar analysis, see
[
HJJY25
]
).

Lemma 2.14

(Local triviality of DHR bimodules)
.

A bimodule
{}_{\mathfrak{A}}Y_{\mathfrak{A}}\in\mathsf{Bim}({\mathfrak{A}})
lies in
\mathsf{DHR}({\mathfrak{A}})
if and only if for any sufficiently large
\Lambda
, the restriction

{}_{{\mathfrak{A}}(\Lambda^{c})}Y_{\mathfrak{A}}

is isomorphic to a summand of a finite direct sum of copies of
{}_{{\mathfrak{A}}(\Lambda^{c})}{\mathfrak{A}}_{\mathfrak{A}}
.

Proof.

Suppose
{}_{\mathfrak{A}}Y_{\mathfrak{A}}\in\mathsf{DHR}({\mathfrak{A}})
and
\{\beta_{i}\}_{i=1}^{n}
is a
Y_{\mathfrak{A}}
-basis localized in
\Lambda
, i.e.,
x\beta_{i}=\beta_{i}x
for all
x\in{\mathfrak{A}}(\Lambda^{c})
.
This condition is identical to saying that the creation operator
L_{\beta_{i}}:{\mathfrak{A}}_{\mathfrak{A}}\to Y_{\mathfrak{A}}
is left
{\mathfrak{A}}(\Lambda^{c})
-linear.
Its adjoint
L_{\beta_{i}}^{\dagger}:Y_{\mathfrak{A}}\to{\mathfrak{A}}_{\mathfrak{A}}
is also left

{\mathfrak{A}}(\Lambda^{c})
-linear, and thus the composite

L^{\dagger}_{\beta_{i}}L_{\beta_{j}}\in{\mathfrak{A}}(\Lambda^{c})^{\prime}\cap{\mathfrak{A}}:=\left\{a\in{\mathfrak{A}}\middle|ax=xa\text{ for all }x\in{\mathfrak{A}}(\Lambda^{c})\right\}.

This implies that the projector
p\in\End({\mathfrak{A}}^{\oplus n}_{\mathfrak{A}})
given by
p_{ij}=\langle\beta_{i}|\beta_{j}\rangle_{\mathfrak{A}}
whose image is isomorphic to
Y_{\mathfrak{A}}

satisfies

p\in{\mathfrak{A}}(\Lambda^{c})^{\prime}\cap M_{n}({\mathfrak{A}})=\End\left({}_{{\mathfrak{A}}(\Lambda^{c})}{\mathfrak{A}}^{\oplus n}_{\mathfrak{A}}\right).

Thus the restriction

{}_{{\mathfrak{A}}(\Lambda^{c})}Y_{\mathfrak{A}}

is isomorphic to a summand of a finite direct sum of copies of
{}_{{\mathfrak{A}}(\Lambda^{c})}{\mathfrak{A}}_{\mathfrak{A}}
.

Conversely, suppose that for any sufficiently large
\Lambda
,
{}_{{\mathfrak{A}}(\Lambda^{c})}Y_{\mathfrak{A}}
is isomorphic to a summand of a finite direct sum of copies of
{}_{{\mathfrak{A}}(\Lambda^{c})}{\mathfrak{A}}_{\mathfrak{A}}
.
This exactly says we have a projector
p\in\End({\mathfrak{A}}^{\oplus n}_{\mathfrak{A}})
which commutes with the left
{\mathfrak{A}}(\Lambda^{c})
-action, and we may identify
Y\cong p{\mathfrak{A}}^{\oplus n}
.
Set
\beta_{i}:=pe_{i}
where
e_{i}
has
i
-th entry 1 and all other entries zero.
Then clearly
\{\beta_{i}\}
is a
p{\mathfrak{A}}^{\oplus n}_{\mathfrak{A}}
-basis such that
x\beta_{i}=\beta_{i}x
for all
x\in{\mathfrak{A}}(\Lambda^{c})
.
Thus
Y
is localizable in every sufficiently large
\Lambda
.
∎

We may use the characterization of DHR bimodules from Lemma
2.14
to compute
\mathsf{DHR}({\mathfrak{A}})
if we understand how such bimodules restrict to
{\mathfrak{A}}(\Lambda^{c})
-bimodules.
The following lemma which relies on dualizability is useful for exactly this type of computation.

Lemma 2.15

(2 out of 3)
.

Suppose
{\mathcal{E}}\subset\mathsf{Bim}(A)
is a fully faithfully embedded and replete unitary multifusion subcategory.
If
X,Z\in\mathsf{Bim}(A)
such that
two out of three of

X,Z,X\boxtimes_{A}Z

lie in
{\mathcal{E}}
, then the third also lies in
{\mathcal{E}}

Proof.

Clearly
X,Z\in{\mathcal{E}}
implies
X\boxtimes_{A}Z\in{\mathcal{E}}
.
We prove
X,X\boxtimes_{A}Z\in{\mathcal{E}}
implies
Z\in{\mathcal{E}}
, and the remaining case is similar.
Observe that
{}_{A}A_{A}
is always a sub-bimodule of
X^{\vee}\boxtimes_{A}X\in{\mathcal{E}}
.
Hence
Z
is a sub-bimodule of

X^{\vee}\boxtimes_{A}X\boxtimes_{A}Z\in{\mathcal{E}}
.
Since
{\mathcal{E}}
is idempotent complete,
Z\in{\mathcal{E}}
.
∎

Example 2.16

(
[
Jon24
, Thm. C]
)
.

Consider the fusion spin chain
{\mathfrak{F}}
build from a UFC with a strong tensor generator
X\in{\mathcal{C}}
(i.e., there is an
n\in{\mathbb{N}}
such that each simple
c\in\Irr({\mathcal{C}})
is a subobject of of
X^{\otimes n}
).
It is straightforward to construct a DHR bimodule
Y^{z}
for every
z\in Z({\mathcal{C}})
via an inductive limit construction.
The main point is that we pick an interval
I
long enough so that every simple of
{\mathcal{C}}
appears as a summand of
X^{\otimes|I|}
,
and then subfactor techniques
for the inclusion of AF
{\mathrm{C}}^{*}
-algebras
{\mathfrak{F}}(I^{c})\subset{\mathfrak{F}}

can be used to construct DHR bimodules.
We will not explain this here, as it is entirely analogous to the module category version in §
3.2
below; instead we refer the reader to
[
Jon24
, §4]
.
It was then shown that
z\mapsto Y^{z}
is a fully faithful braided tensor functor using the Ocneanu Compactness Theorem
[
JS97
]
(see also
[
BCE+25
]
and
[
DGGJ22
]
).
We give a generalization of this construction and the proof that the functor is fully faithful in Appendix
A
below.

To see that this functor is essentially surjective, for an arbitrary
Y\in\mathsf{DHR}({\mathfrak{F}})
,

{}_{{\mathfrak{F}}(I^{c})}Y_{\mathfrak{F}}
is a summand of a direct sum of the trivial bimodule
{}_{{\mathfrak{F}}(I^{c})}{\mathfrak{F}}_{\mathfrak{F}}
by Lemma
2.14
.
We then restrict the right action to see that

{}_{{\mathfrak{F}}(I^{c})}Y_{{\mathfrak{F}}(I^{c})}
is a summand of a direct sum of the trivial bimodule
{}_{{\mathfrak{F}}(I^{c})}{\mathfrak{F}}_{{\mathfrak{F}}(I^{c})}
.
These trivial bimodules lie in the essential image of
{\mathcal{C}}\boxtimes{\mathcal{C}}^{\rm mp}
in
\mathsf{Bim}({\mathfrak{F}}(I^{c}))
by using the
Q-system realization
technique from
[
CHPJP22
]
.
One then induces back to
\mathsf{Bim}({\mathfrak{F}})
using Lemma
2.15
to conclude that
{}_{\mathfrak{F}}Y_{\mathfrak{F}}
is in the essential image of
Z({\mathcal{C}})
.
Here, we have used the fact that one can embed the unitary multifusion category

{\mathcal{E}}=\begin{pmatrix}{\mathcal{C}}\boxtimes{\mathcal{C}}^{\rm mp}&{\mathcal{C}}\\
{\mathcal{C}}^{\rm op}&Z({\mathcal{C}})\end{pmatrix}

fully faithfully into
\mathsf{Bim}({\mathfrak{F}}(I^{c})\oplus{\mathfrak{F}})
.
Thus Lemma
2.15
is applied twice with
A={\mathfrak{F}}(I^{c})\oplus{\mathfrak{F}}
.

2.4.
Boundary LTO axioms for a net of algebras on a lattice with boundary

We now consider a net of algebras
{\mathfrak{A}}
on a lattice with boundary.
We consider the lattice
{\mathcal{L}}={\mathbb{Z}}^{d}\times{\mathbb{N}}

where
\partial{\mathcal{L}}:={\mathbb{Z}}^{d}\times\{0\}
is considered as a distinguished 1D boundary.
We write
{\mathcal{L}}^{\circ}:={\mathcal{L}}\setminus\partial{\mathcal{L}}={\mathbb{Z}}^{d}\times\{1,2,3,4,\dots\}
.

As above, our net of algebras
{\mathfrak{A}}
on our lattice with boundary is equipped with a net of projections
\Lambda\mapsto p_{\Lambda}
ordered by reverse inclusion.
For rectangles suitably far away from
\partial{\mathcal{L}}
, we require the above
(LTO1)
–
(LTO4)
axioms for the bulk.
For rectangles along the boundary, we must now allow for surrounding rectangles to intersect on two adjacent sides, rather than along only one side.

Definition 2.17
.

We say a rectangle
\Lambda
with
\partial\Lambda\cap\partial{\mathcal{L}}\neq\emptyset
is:

•

completely

\partial
-
surrounded
by
\Delta
with surrounding constant
s
, denoted
\Lambda\ll_{s}^{\partial}\Delta
, if

\Lambda\subset\Delta
,
\partial\Lambda\cap\partial\Delta
is a rectangle one dimension lower which lies in
\partial{\mathcal{L}}
, and for all other points
v\in\Delta
not in
\Lambda
, an
\ell^{\infty}
ball of radius
s
containing
v
fits inside
\Delta
.

Alternatively,
\Lambda\ll_{s}^{\partial}\Delta
if and only if
\Lambda\Subset_{s}\Delta
with
\emptyset\neq\partial\Lambda\cap\partial\Delta\subset\partial{\mathcal{L}}
.

•

\partial
-
surrounded
by
\Delta
with surrounding constant
s
, denoted
\Lambda\Subset_{s}^{\partial}\Delta
, if
\Lambda\subset\Delta
,
\partial\Lambda\cap\partial\Delta
is the union of two rectangles of one dimension lower that intersect each other, one of which lies in
\partial{\mathcal{L}}
, and for all other points
v\in\Delta
not in
\Lambda
, an
\ell^{\infty}
ball of radius
s
containing
v
fits inside
\Delta
.

\Delta
\Lambda
\partial{\mathcal{L}}
{\mathcal{L}}^{\circ}
\Lambda\ll_{1}^{\partial}\Delta

\Delta
\Lambda
\partial{\mathcal{L}}
{\mathcal{L}}^{\circ}
\Lambda\Subset_{1}^{\partial}\Delta

For a rectangle
\Lambda
intersecting
\partial{\mathcal{L}}
and a rectangle
\Delta
with
\Lambda\Subset_{s}^{\partial}\Delta
, we introduce the ‘corner’ boundary algebra

{\mathfrak{B}}^{\partial}(\Lambda\Subset_{s}^{\partial}\Delta)
defined exactly as in the case
{\mathfrak{B}}(\Lambda\Subset_{s}\Delta)
.
The following
boundary LTO axioms
ensure that this algebra is independent of choices beyond the intersection of the rectangles (see §
2.5
below for an outline of the argument).

(
\partial
LTO1)

Whenever
\Lambda\ll_{s}^{\partial}\Delta
,
p_{\Delta}{\mathfrak{A}}(\Lambda)p_{\Delta}={\mathbb{C}}p_{\Delta}
.

(
\partial
LTO2)

Whenever
\Lambda\Subset_{s}^{\delta}\Delta
,
p_{\Delta}{\mathfrak{A}}(\Lambda)p_{\Delta}={\mathfrak{B}}^{\partial}(\Lambda\Subset_{s}^{\delta}\Delta)p_{\Delta}
.

(
\partial
LTO3)

Whenever

\Lambda_{1}\subset\Lambda_{2}\Subset_{s}^{\delta}\Delta
with

\partial\Lambda_{1}\cap\partial\Delta=\partial\Lambda_{2}\cap\partial\Delta
,

{\mathfrak{B}}^{\partial}(\Lambda_{1}\Subset_{s}^{\delta}\Delta)={\mathfrak{B}}^{\partial}(\Lambda_{2}\Subset_{s}^{\delta}\Delta)
.

(
\partial
LTO4)

Whenever
\Lambda\Subset_{s}^{\delta}\Delta_{1}\subset\Delta_{2}
with

\partial\Lambda\cap\partial\Delta_{1}=\partial\Lambda\cap\partial\Delta_{2}
,
the map
x\mapsto xp_{\Delta_{2}}
is injective.

Example 2.18
.

Kitaev’s Toric Code with smooth boundary satisfies
(

∂

LTO1)
–
(

∂

LTO4)
.
Indeed, for rectangles
\Lambda
such that
\partial\Lambda
meets the smooth boundary, our projection
p_{\Lambda}
is still given by

p_{\Lambda}:=\prod_{s\subset\Lambda}\left(\frac{1+A_{s}}{2}\right)\prod_{p\subset\Lambda}\left(\frac{1+B_{p}}{2}\right),

but we now have more terms
A_{s}
and
B_{p}
than before in our boundary Hamiltonian.
Indeed, every boundary star and plaquette

\scriptstyle\sigma^{Z}
B_{p}
\scriptstyle\sigma^{X}
\scriptstyle\sigma^{X}
\scriptstyle\sigma^{X}
A_{s}
\Lambda

is included in the boundary Hamiltonian, so the argument in
[
JNPW23
, §3]
based on
[
AFH07
]
now implies that
(

∂

LTO1)
holds.
The axioms
(

∂

LTO2)
–
(

∂

LTO4)
can be similarly adapted from the proofs in
[
JNPW23
, §3]
.

Similarly, Kitaev’s Toric Code with rough boundary also satisfies
(

∂

LTO1)
–
(

∂

LTO4)
.

Example 2.19
.

We will see in §
3
below that the 1D boundary for the 2D Levin-Wen model for
{\mathcal{C}}
coming from an indecomposable module category
{\mathcal{M}}_{\mathcal{C}}
satisfies
(

∂

LTO1)
–
(

∂

LTO4)
.

2.5.
Boundary algebras and DHR bimodules for boundary LTOs

Similar to the construction of the boundary net of algebras
{\mathfrak{B}}
from the net
{\mathfrak{A}}

from a choice of codimension one sub-lattice
along with the quantum channel
{\mathbb{E}}:{\mathfrak{A}}_{{\mathbb{H}}}\to{\mathfrak{B}}
,
for a lattice with boundary
{\mathcal{L}}

and a sublattice with boundary
{\mathcal{K}}
such that

\partial{\mathcal{K}}\subset\partial{\mathcal{L}}

but
{\mathcal{K}}
is not completely contained in
{\mathcal{L}}

and a choice of ‘quadrant’
{\mathbb{Q}}\subset{\mathcal{L}}
on one side of
{\mathcal{K}}
(so that
{\mathcal{K}}\subset\partial{\mathbb{Q}}
),

\partial{\mathcal{K}}
{\mathcal{K}}
\partial{\mathcal{L}}
{\mathbb{Q}}

we get a boundary net of algebras
{\mathfrak{B}}^{\partial}
on
{\mathcal{K}}
together with a quantum channel
{\mathfrak{A}}_{\mathbb{Q}}\to{\mathfrak{B}}^{\partial}
.

Similar to
[
JNPW23
, Lem. 2.13]
, the axioms
(

∂

LTO1)
–
(

∂

LTO4)
above ensure that
{\mathfrak{B}}^{\partial}(\Lambda\Subset_{s}^{\delta}\Delta)
is independent of the choice of
\Lambda\Subset_{s}^{\delta}\Delta\subset{\mathbb{Q}}
beyond the intersection
I:=\partial\Lambda\cap\partial\Delta\cap{\mathcal{K}}
.
Indeed, we may choose
\Lambda_{I}\subset\Lambda
to be the smallest sufficiently large rectangle with
\partial\Lambda_{I}\cap{\mathcal{K}}=I
and
\Delta_{I}\subset\Delta
to be the smallest rectangle with
\Lambda_{I}\Subset_{s}^{\partial}\Delta_{I}
and
\partial\Lambda_{I}\cap\partial\Delta_{I}=I
.
We then define

{\mathfrak{B}}^{\partial}(I):={\mathfrak{B}}^{\partial}(\Lambda_{I}\Subset_{s}\Delta_{I}),

and the map
I\mapsto{\mathfrak{B}}^{\partial}(I)
defines a net of algebras with boundary on
{\mathcal{K}}
.

We now introduce the notion of a
boundary DHR bimodule
for a net of algebras
{\mathfrak{A}}
on a lattice
{\mathcal{L}}
with boundary
\partial{\mathcal{L}}
, which is localized near the boundary
\partial{\mathcal{L}}
.
(We will use this notion for the boundary algebra
{\mathfrak{B}}^{\partial}
on
{\mathcal{K}}
, which has boundary
\partial{\mathcal{K}}={\mathcal{K}}\cap\partial{\mathcal{L}}
.)

Definition 2.20
.

A
boundary DHR bimodule
for
{\mathfrak{A}}
is an
{\mathfrak{A}}-{\mathfrak{A}}
Hilbert
{\mathrm{C}}^{*}
-correspondence
{}_{{\mathfrak{A}}}Y_{{\mathfrak{A}}}
such that
for any sufficiently large rectangle
\Lambda\subset{\mathcal{L}}
which meets
\partial{\mathcal{L}}
,
Y
is localized in
\Lambda
in the sense of Definition
2.12
above.
Unpacking, this means there is a finite
Y_{{\mathfrak{A}}}
-basis
\{\beta_{i}\}\subset Y
such that
\beta_{i}a=a\beta_{i}
for all

a\in{\mathfrak{A}}(\Lambda^{c}):=\varinjlim_{\Delta\subset\Lambda^{c}}{\mathfrak{A}}(\Delta)\subset{\mathfrak{A}}.

That is, the basis elements
\beta_{i}
commute with all the elements of
{\mathfrak{A}}
which are in the subalgebra supported on
\Lambda^{c}
.

We denote the full subcategory of boundary DHR-bimodules by
\mathsf{DHR}^{\partial}({\mathfrak{A}})\subset\mathsf{Bim}({\mathfrak{A}})
.
Observe that
\mathsf{DHR}^{\partial}({\mathfrak{A}})
is closed under composition of bimodules and thus forms a full
{\mathrm{C}}^{*}
tensor subcategory.

Similar to Lemma
2.14
above, we have the following characterization of boundary DHR bimodules whose proof is identical and therefore omitted.

Lemma 2.21

(Local triviality of boundary DHR bimodules)
.

A bimodule
{}_{{\mathfrak{A}}}Y_{{\mathfrak{A}}}\in\mathsf{Bim}({\mathfrak{A}})
lies in
\mathsf{DHR}^{\partial}({\mathfrak{A}})
if and only if for any sufficiently large
\Lambda
which meets
\partial{\mathcal{L}}
, the restriction

{}_{{\mathfrak{A}}(\Lambda^{c})}Y_{{\mathfrak{A}}}

is isomorphic to a summand of a finite direct sum of copies of
{}_{{\mathfrak{A}}(\Lambda^{c})}{\mathfrak{A}}_{{\mathfrak{A}}}
.

Even though our net of algebras on our lattice with boundary may no longer satisfy algebraic Haag duality (e.g., the fusion module categorical net in §
3.2
below does not have this property), we still have a notion of
boundary algebraic Haag duality
.
(There are obvious weaker/bounded spread variants of this notion, which we leave to the reader.)

Definition 2.22
.

A net of algebras
{\mathfrak{A}}
on a lattice with boundary satisfies
boundary algebraic Haag duality
if for every rectangle
\Delta
meeting the boundary
\partial{\mathcal{L}}
,

Z_{{\mathfrak{A}}}({\mathfrak{A}}(\Delta^{c}))={\mathfrak{A}}(\Delta)
,
where again
{\mathfrak{A}}(\Delta^{c})
is the subalgebra of
{\mathfrak{A}}
generated by the
{\mathfrak{A}}(\Lambda)
with
\Lambda\subset\Delta^{c}
.

The proof of the following lemma is identical to Lemma
2.10
.

Lemma 2.23
.

If
\eta,\xi\in Y\in\mathsf{Bim}^{\partial}({\mathfrak{A}})
are both localized in
\Delta
which meets
\partial{\mathcal{L}}
and
a\in{\mathfrak{A}}(\Delta)
, then

\langle\eta|a\xi\rangle_{{\mathfrak{A}}}\in Z_{{\mathfrak{A}}}({\mathfrak{A}}(\Lambda))
for all
\Lambda\subset\Delta^{c}
.
In particular, if
{\mathfrak{A}}
satisfies boundary algebraic Haag duality, then
\langle\eta|a\xi\rangle_{{\mathfrak{A}}}\in{\mathfrak{A}}(\Delta)
.

The tensor category
\mathsf{DHR}^{\partial}({\mathfrak{A}})
does not have a braiding.
We expect that one can adapt the definition of the braiding on
\mathsf{DHR}({\mathfrak{A}})
to get a canonical
half-braiding
for the image of
\mathsf{DHR}({\mathfrak{A}})
in
\mathsf{DHR}^{\partial}({\mathfrak{A}})
with
\mathsf{DHR}^{\partial}({\mathfrak{A}})
.
We leave this exploration for a future article as it would take us too far afield.

3.
Boundary LTO for Levin-Wen

In this section, we construct a boundary LTO from the boundary Levin-Wen model
[
KK12
]
built from a unitary fusion category (UFC)
{\mathcal{C}}
and an indecomposable unitary module category
{\mathcal{M}}_{\mathcal{C}}
.
We work with a unitary tensor category version of this model along the lines of
[
Kon14
,
GHK+24
]

rather than the 6j symbol model.
To do so, let us first recall our notation.
We denote the unique unitary spherical dual functor of
{\mathcal{C}}
by
\vee
, and we write
d_{c}:=\tr^{\mathcal{C}}(\id_{c})
.
We write
\Irr({\mathcal{C}})
for a set of representatives for the simple objects of
{\mathcal{C}}
, and we write
D_{\mathcal{C}}:=\sum_{c\in\Irr({\mathcal{C}})}d_{c}^{2}
.
For our module category
{\mathcal{M}}
, we write
\Irr({\mathcal{M}})
for a set of representatives for the simple objects of
{\mathcal{M}}
.

Our indecomposable unitary module category
{\mathcal{M}}
is equipped with a unitary
module trace

\Tr^{\mathcal{M}}
, which consists of a family of faithful positive linear functionals

\Tr^{\mathcal{M}}_{m}:{\mathcal{M}}(m\to m)\to{\mathbb{C}}
for each
m\in{\mathcal{M}}
satisfying

\Tr^{\mathcal{M}}_{m}(g\circ f)=\Tr^{\mathcal{M}}_{n}(f\circ g)\qquad\qquad\qquad\forall\,f,g:m\to n,\quad\forall\,m,n\in{\mathcal{M}},

and for all
h:m\lhd c\to m\lhd c
, we have

By
[
Sch13
]
,
\Tr^{\mathcal{M}}
is unique up to positive scalar.
This scalar will be chosen judiciously later on; the curious reader may read Appendix
A
first if they desire.
We write
d_{m}:=\Tr^{\mathcal{M}}_{m}(\id_{m})
, and note that in our conventions,
\sum_{m\in\Irr({\mathcal{M}})}d_{m}^{2}\neq D_{\mathcal{C}}
in general.

3.1.
The boundary Levin-Wen model

For simplicity we will only consider the model on a square lattice in two dimensions with a 1D boundary.
The Hilbert space can be visualized as follows, where the black edges carry labels from
\Irr({\mathcal{C}})
and the blue edges carry labels from
\Irr({\mathcal{M}})
.

{\mathcal{L}}
\partial{\mathcal{L}}

Here, we read from bottom left to top right.

Consider now a 2D rectangle
\Lambda
in our lattice
{\mathcal{L}}
.
We consider the canonical spin system from this setup, i.e., we define local algebras

{\mathfrak{A}}(\Lambda):=\bigotimes_{v\in\Lambda}B({\mathcal{H}}_{v})
.
We set
{\mathfrak{A}}:=\varinjlim{\mathfrak{A}}(\Lambda)=\bigotimes_{v}B({\mathcal{H}}_{v})
.
There are edge terms
A_{\ell}
which enforce that the simple labels on connected edges match, and there are plaquette terms
B_{p}
for every square in the lattice, pictured below.

For plaquettes meeting the boundary, we must use the module action to resolve the diagram into the local Hilbert spaces.
The result
[
GHK+24
, Lem. 2.8]
(see also
[
Hon09
, §5]
,
[
Kon14
, §5]
) provides a formula for the matrix coefficients
C(\xi,\xi^{\prime})
for the
B_{p}
operators in the bulk in terms of diagrams in the associated
skein module
which shows these operators are self-adjoint projectors.
A similar formula holds along the boundary.

In more detail,
the skein module for
{\mathcal{C}}
with
n
boundary points, denoted
{\mathcal{S}}_{\mathcal{C}}(n)
, is the Hilbert space

{\mathcal{C}}(1_{\mathcal{C}}\to X^{\otimes n})=\bigoplus_{x_{1},\dots,x_{n}\in\Irr({\mathcal{C}})}{\mathcal{C}}(1_{\mathcal{C}}\to x_{1}\otimes\cdots\otimes x_{n})

where the direct sum is orthogonal,
and each subspace
{\mathcal{C}}(1_{\mathcal{C}}\to x_{1}\otimes\cdots\otimes x_{n})
has inner product

The square roots of dimensions are included in the denominator to ensure that gluing of morphisms is isometric as in
[
GHK+24
, Lem. 2.4]
.

We define

p^{A}_{\Lambda}:=\prod_{\ell\subset\Lambda}A_{\ell}
,

p^{B}_{\Lambda}:=\prod_{p\subset\ell}B_{p}
, and
p_{\Lambda}:=p^{A}_{\Lambda}p^{B}_{\Lambda}
.
We have the following theorem for the operator
p^{B}_{\Lambda}
on
p^{A}_{\Lambda}\bigotimes_{v\in\Lambda}{\mathcal{H}}_{v}
.

Lemma 3.4

(
[
Kon14
]
,
[
GHK+24
, Thm. 2.9]
)
.

For a rectangle
\Lambda
contained in the bulk, on the subspace
p^{A}_{\Lambda}\bigotimes_{v\in\Lambda}{\mathcal{H}}_{v}
,

p^{B}_{\Lambda}=D_{{\mathcal{C}}}^{-\#p\subset\Lambda}\cdot\eval_{\mathcal{C}}^{\dagger}\circ\eval_{\mathcal{C}},

where
\#p\subset\Lambda
is the number of plaquettes in
\Lambda

and
\eval_{\mathcal{C}}
is the evaluation map from the image of
p_{A}^{\Lambda}
to the skein module
{\mathcal{S}}_{\mathcal{C}}(\#\partial\Lambda)
.
Hence
p_{\Lambda}\bigotimes_{v\in\Lambda}{\mathcal{H}}_{v}
is unitarily isomorphic to
{\mathcal{S}}_{\mathcal{C}}(\#\partial\Lambda)
via the map
D_{{\mathcal{C}}}^{-\#p\subset\Lambda/2}\eval_{\mathcal{C}}
.

This result was used in
[
JNPW23
]
to prove that the net of projections
(p_{\Lambda})
for the 2D Levin-Wen model without boundary
satisfies the LTO axioms from
[
JNPW23
]
(see §
2.1
above for the main definitions).
In order to extend this to the boundary Levin-Wen model, we have similar result for rectangles which meet the boundary.

Lemma 3.5
.

For a rectangle
\Lambda
such that
\partial\Lambda\cap\partial{\mathcal{L}}\neq\emptyset
, on
p^{A}_{\Lambda}\bigotimes_{v\in\Lambda}{\mathcal{H}}_{v}
,

p^{B}_{\Lambda}=D_{{\mathcal{C}}}^{-\#p\subset\Lambda}\cdot\eval_{\mathcal{M}}^{\dagger}\circ\eval_{\mathcal{M}},

where
\#p\subset\Lambda
is the number of plaquettes in
\Lambda

and
\eval_{\mathcal{M}}
is the evaulation map from the image of
p_{A}^{\Lambda}
to the skein module
{\mathcal{S}}_{\mathcal{M}}(\#\partial\Lambda)
.
Hence
p_{\Lambda}\bigotimes_{v\in\Lambda}{\mathcal{H}}_{v}
is unitarily isomorphic to
{\mathcal{S}}_{\mathcal{M}}(\#\partial\Lambda)
via the map
D_{{\mathcal{C}}}^{-\#p\subset\Lambda/2}\eval_{\mathcal{M}}
.

Definition 3.6
.

We now cut our 2D region along a horizontal 1D slice as in (
3.7
) below.
We denote the 1D slice by
{\mathcal{K}}
.
For a 2D rectangle
\Lambda
contained in the bottom half-space bounded by
{\mathcal{K}}
, we let
I=I(\Lambda)
be the intersection
\partial\Lambda\cap{\mathcal{K}}
.
Observe that
I=\emptyset
if
\Lambda\cap{\mathcal{K}}=\emptyset
.
When
I\neq\emptyset
, we define

{\mathfrak{M}}(I):=\begin{cases}\End_{\mathcal{C}}(X^{\otimes I})&\text{if }I\cap\partial{\mathcal{L}}=\emptyset\\
\End_{\mathcal{M}}(W\lhd X^{\otimes I\setminus\partial{\mathcal{L}}})&\text{if }I\cap\partial{\mathcal{L}}\neq\emptyset\end{cases}

where
X^{\otimes I}
is the tensor product of the
generator
X=\bigoplus_{c\in\Irr({\mathcal{C}})}c\in{\mathcal{C}}
over the sites in
I
,

X^{\otimes I\setminus\partial{\mathcal{L}}}
means taking the tensor product over the sites in
I\setminus\partial{\mathcal{L}}
,
and

W=\bigoplus_{m\in\Irr({\mathcal{M}})}m\in{\mathcal{M}}
as above.
In (
3.7
) below,
I
is
the interval where
\partial\Lambda
intersects the red slice, so points in
I
are oriented from
left-to-right
.
For example:

(3.7)

\scriptstyle{\mathcal{K}}
\scriptstyle I
\Lambda
\rightsquigarrow
{\mathfrak{M}}(I)=\End_{\mathcal{C}}(X^{\otimes 2})
\scriptstyle J
\Delta
\rightsquigarrow
{\mathfrak{M}}(J)=\End_{\mathcal{M}}(W\lhd X^{\otimes 4})

We call the 1D net of algebras with boundary
{\mathfrak{M}}
the
fusion module categorical net
associated to
{\mathcal{M}}_{{\mathcal{C}}}
with generators
X\in{\mathcal{C}}
and
W\in{\mathcal{M}}
.

When
\partial\Lambda\cap{\mathcal{K}}\neq\emptyset
but
\partial\Lambda\cap\partial{\mathcal{L}}=\emptyset
,
just as
[
JNPW23
, Def. 4.6]
, for
\varphi\in\End_{\mathcal{C}}(X^{\otimes I})
, we can define a gluing operator
\Gamma_{\varphi}
acting on
\bigotimes_{v\in\Lambda}{\mathcal{H}}_{v}
.
When
I
is as in (
3.7
) and

\varphi\in{\mathcal{C}}(\bigotimes_{I}a_{i}\to\bigotimes_{I}b_{i})
,
\Gamma_{\varphi}
first applies the projector
p_{\Lambda}
so that the edge labels of the vectors match and plaquettes are effectively filled.
This allows us to view a vector in
p_{\Lambda}\bigotimes_{v\in\Lambda}{\mathcal{H}}_{v}

as an element of the skein module
{\mathcal{S}}_{\mathcal{C}}(\#\partial\Lambda)
, giving an element in
{\mathcal{C}}(1\to X^{\otimes\partial\Lambda})
.
We can then take our desired morphism
\varphi
and glue it on, first projecting to make sure the labels
a_{i}
in
\bigotimes_{I}a_{i}
match so that composition is well-defined.
In order for this action to be a
*
-action, we also multiply by a ratio of quantum dimensions to the
1/4
power; we refer the reader to
[
GHK+24
, Eq. (2)]
for further details.

{\mathfrak{B}}(\Lambda\Subset\Delta)=\left\{\Gamma_{\varphi}\middle|\varphi\in\End_{\mathcal{C}}(X^{\otimes I})\right\}\cong{\mathfrak{M}}(I)\qquad\qquad I=\partial\Delta\cap\partial\Lambda\cap{\mathcal{K}}

,

.

As before, this new morphism from
{\mathcal{M}}
must be resolved into a vector in
\bigotimes_{v\in\Lambda}{\mathcal{H}}_{v}
in the usual way using semisimplicity.

Arguing as in
[
JNPW23
, Lem. 4.7 and Thm. 4.8]
, but using a variant of the strip/ladder algebra for
{\mathcal{M}}_{{\mathcal{C}}}

from
[
KK12
,
BBJ19
]

instead of the tube algebra, we get the following theorem.

Theorem 3.8
.

The boundary Levin-Wen model for
{\mathcal{M}}_{\mathcal{C}}
satisfies
(

∂

LTO1)
–
(

∂

LTO4)
for
s=1

and the boundary algebra

{\mathfrak{B}}(\Lambda\Subset^{\delta}\Delta)=\left\{\Gamma_{\psi}\middle|\psi\in\End_{\mathcal{M}}(W\lhd X^{\otimes J\setminus\partial{\mathcal{L}}})\right\}\cong{\mathfrak{M}}(J)\qquad\qquad J=\partial\Lambda\cap\partial\Delta\cap{\mathcal{K}}

is isomorphic to the fusion module categorical net for
{\mathcal{M}}_{{\mathcal{C}}}
with generators
X\in{\mathcal{C}}
and
W\in{\mathcal{M}}
.

3.2.
The boundary DHR theory for the boundary Levin-Wen model

We now analyze the boundary DHR theory for our boundary Levin-Wen model using subfactor theory.
We denote the fusion module boundary algebra by

{\mathfrak{M}}:=\varinjlim_{n}\End_{\mathcal{M}}(W\lhd X^{\otimes n}).

We now unpack Definition
2.20
of the tensor category
\mathsf{DHR}^{\partial}({\mathfrak{M}})
of boundary DHR bimodules for
{\mathfrak{M}}
.
Such a bimodule is an
{\mathfrak{M}}-{\mathfrak{M}}
Hilbert
{\mathrm{C}}^{*}
-correspondence
{}_{\mathfrak{M}}Y_{\mathfrak{M}}
such that there is an interval
I\subset{\mathcal{K}}
which meets the boundary (
I\cap\partial{\mathcal{L}}\neq\emptyset
) such that
Y
is
localizable
in
I
, i.e., there is a finite
Y_{\mathfrak{M}}
-basis
\{\beta_{i}\}\subset Y
such that
\beta_{i}a=a\beta_{i}
for all

a\in{\mathfrak{M}}(I^{c}):=\varinjlim_{k}\End_{\mathcal{C}}(X^{\otimes k})\subset\varinjlim_{k}\End_{\mathcal{M}}(W\lhd X^{\otimes|I-1|+k})={\mathfrak{M}}

That is, the basis elements
\beta_{i}
commute with all the elements of
{\mathfrak{M}}
which are in the subalgebra supported on
I^{c}
.

Construction 3.9
.

We construct for each
F\in\End({\mathcal{M}}_{\mathcal{C}})
a DHR bimodule
{}_{\mathfrak{M}}Y^{F}_{\mathfrak{M}}
.
We then show that the bimodules
Y^{F}
assemble into a fully faithful tensor functor

(3.10)

Y:\End({\mathcal{M}}_{\mathcal{C}})\to\mathsf{DHR}^{\partial}({\mathfrak{M}}).

For
n\geq 0
, we define

Y^{F}_{n}:={\mathcal{M}}(W\lhd X^{\otimes n}\to FW\lhd\otimes X^{\otimes n})

which is naturally a bimodule for
{\mathfrak{M}}_{n}:=\End_{\mathcal{M}}(W\lhd X^{\otimes n})
, where
the left action is post-composition after applying
F
and the right action is pre-composition.
We equip
Y^{F}_{n}
with a right
{\mathfrak{M}}_{n}
-valued inner product by

\langle\eta|\xi\rangle_{{\mathfrak{M}}_{n}}:=\eta^{\dagger}\circ\xi\in\End(({\mathfrak{M}}_{n})_{{\mathfrak{M}}_{n}})={\mathfrak{M}}_{n}.

Observe that the inclusions
-\otimes\id_{X}:Y^{F}_{n}\hookrightarrow Y^{F}_{n+1}

are compatible with the inclusions
-\otimes\id_{X}:{\mathfrak{M}}_{n}\hookrightarrow{\mathfrak{M}}_{n+1}
, and that

\langle\eta\otimes\id_{X}|\xi\otimes\id_{X}\rangle_{{\mathfrak{M}}_{n+1}}=(\eta\otimes\id_{X})^{\dagger}\circ(\xi\otimes\id_{X})=\eta^{\dagger}\circ\xi\otimes\id_{X}=\langle\eta|\xi\rangle_{{\mathfrak{M}}_{n}}\otimes\id_{X}.

We thus get an inductive limit
{\mathfrak{M}}-{\mathfrak{M}}
bimodule
Y^{F}:=\varinjlim Y^{F}_{n}
.

Now for each
{\mathcal{C}}
-module natural transformation
\theta:F\Rightarrow G
in
\End({\mathcal{M}}_{\mathcal{C}})
, we get a bimodule intertwiner as the inductive limit of the maps

{\mathcal{M}}(W\lhd X^{\otimes n}\to FW\lhd\otimes X^{\otimes n})=Y_{n}^{F}\ni f\mapsto(\theta_{W}\otimes\id_{X^{\otimes n}})\circ f\in Y_{n}^{G}={\mathcal{M}}(W\lhd X^{\otimes n}\to GW\lhd\otimes X^{\otimes n}).

This construction is easily seen to be a unitary tensor functor.
Moreover, it can be shown that this functor is fully faithful using the unitary multifusion category embedding results of
[
BCE+25
]
, together with the
Q-system realization
technique from
[
CHPJP22
]
.
We review this argument in the context of
{\mathrm{C}}^{*}
-Hilbert bimodules in Appendix
A
below for convenience of the reader.

Remark 3.11
.

Appendix
A
proves far more than the fully faithfulness of the unitary tensor functor

\End({\mathcal{M}}_{\mathcal{C}})\hookrightarrow\mathsf{Bim}({\mathfrak{M}})
given by
F\mapsto Y^{F}
.
We may think of
\End({\mathcal{M}}_{\mathcal{C}})
as one corner of a unitary multifusion category which also includes
{\mathcal{C}},{\mathcal{M}}
:

{\mathcal{E}}:=\begin{pmatrix}\End({\mathcal{M}}_{\mathcal{C}})&{\mathcal{M}}\\
{\mathcal{M}}^{\rm op}&{\mathcal{C}}\end{pmatrix}.

Similar to the above construction, we may also embed
{\mathcal{C}}
fully faithfully as
{\mathrm{C}}^{*}
-Hilbert bimodules over the inductive limit algebra

{\mathfrak{N}}:=\varinjlim_{k}\End_{\mathcal{C}}(X^{\otimes k}),

and similarly, we can embed
{\mathcal{M}}
fully faithfully as
{\mathfrak{M}}-{\mathfrak{N}}
bimodules.
All told, this produces a fully faithful unitary tensor functor

{\mathcal{E}}:=\begin{pmatrix}\End({\mathcal{M}}_{\mathcal{C}})&{\mathcal{M}}\\
{\mathcal{M}}^{\rm op}&{\mathcal{C}}\end{pmatrix}\hookrightarrow\begin{pmatrix}\mathsf{Bim}({\mathfrak{M}})&\mathsf{Bim}({\mathfrak{M}},{\mathfrak{N}})\\
\mathsf{Bim}({\mathfrak{N}},{\mathfrak{M}})&\mathsf{Bim}({\mathfrak{N}})\end{pmatrix}=\mathsf{Bim}({\mathfrak{M}}\oplus{\mathfrak{N}}).

Indeed, one first uses the results of
[
BCE+25
]
to fully faithfully embed
{\mathcal{C}}
into
\mathsf{Bim}({\mathfrak{N}})
.
The Q-system realization technique then allows one to boost this embedding into a fully faithful embedding of the unitary multifusion category of
Q-Q
bimodules
{}_{Q}{\mathcal{C}}_{Q}
into
\mathsf{Bim}(|Q|_{{\mathfrak{N}}})
, the Hilbert
{\mathrm{C}}^{*}
-bimodules over the realized Q-system.
Choosing
Q=1\oplus\underline{\End}_{\mathcal{C}}(W)
using the unitary internal end
[
HPT24
,
CFH+24
]
, we have
{}_{Q}{\mathcal{C}}_{Q}\cong{\mathcal{E}}
and
|Q|_{\mathfrak{N}}\cong{\mathfrak{M}}\oplus{\mathfrak{N}}
, as claimed.

Moreover, we do not need that
{\mathcal{C}}
is fusion nor that
{\mathcal{M}}
is indecomposable; this construction works for arbitrary unitary multifusion
{\mathcal{C}}
and unitary modules
{\mathcal{M}}_{\mathcal{C}}
.
However, one must choose the unitary module trace on
{\mathcal{M}}
carefully to be compatible with the generator
W\in{\mathcal{M}}
.

We refer the reader to Appendix
A
for a more detailed discussion.

Notation 3.12
.

For an interval
I\subset{\mathcal{K}}
which meets
\partial{\mathcal{L}}
,
we write
{\mathfrak{N}}_{I}:={\mathfrak{M}}(I^{c})
, so that we have a canonical inclusion

\iota_{I}:=1_{{\mathfrak{M}}(I)}\otimes-:{\mathfrak{N}}_{I}\hookrightarrow{\mathfrak{M}}
.
The algebra
{\mathfrak{N}}_{I}
is the relative commutant of
{\mathfrak{M}}(I)
in
{\mathfrak{M}}
.
Observe that for all
I
, the algebras
{\mathfrak{N}}_{I}
are obviously isomorphic to

{\mathfrak{N}}:=\varinjlim_{k}\End_{\mathcal{C}}(X^{\otimes k}).

The algebra
{\mathfrak{M}}
is naturally an
{\mathfrak{N}}_{I}-{\mathfrak{N}}_{I}
Hilbert
{\mathrm{C}}^{*}
-bimodule using the Q-system realization technique for the Q-system

\underline{\End}_{\mathcal{C}}(W\lhd X^{\otimes|I|-1})\in{\mathcal{C}}
.
Hence
{}_{{\mathfrak{N}}_{I}}{\mathfrak{M}}_{{\mathfrak{N}}_{I}}
lies in the fully faithful image of
{\mathcal{C}}\subset\mathsf{Bim}({\mathfrak{N}}_{I})\cong\mathsf{Bim}({\mathfrak{N}})
.
Moreover, the centralizer

(3.13)

Z_{\mathfrak{M}}({\mathfrak{N}}_{I})=\End_{{\mathfrak{N}}_{I}-{\mathfrak{M}}}({\mathfrak{M}})\cong\End_{\mathcal{M}}(W\lhd X^{\otimes|I|-1})={\mathfrak{M}}(I),

i.e., the fusion module categorical net satisfies boundary algebraic Haag duality.
Again, more details can be found in Appendix
A
.

Theorem 3.14
.

The category
\mathsf{DHR}^{\partial}({\mathfrak{M}})
of boundary DHR bimodules is the essential image of
\End({\mathcal{M}}_{\mathcal{C}})\subseteq\mathsf{DHR}^{\partial}({\mathfrak{M}})
.

Proof.

Suppose
{}_{\mathfrak{M}}Y_{\mathfrak{M}}\in\mathsf{DHR}^{\partial}({\mathfrak{M}})
.
Since
Y
is localized in some boundary interval
I
, by Lemma
2.14
,
the restriction
{}_{{\mathfrak{N}}_{I}}Y_{\mathfrak{M}}={}_{{\mathfrak{N}}_{I}}{\mathfrak{M}}\boxtimes_{\mathfrak{M}}Y_{\mathfrak{M}}
is isomorphic to a summand of a finite direct sum of copies of
{}_{{\mathfrak{N}}_{I}}{\mathfrak{M}}_{\mathfrak{M}}
, which lies in the essential image of
{\mathcal{E}}
in
\mathsf{Bim}({\mathfrak{M}}\oplus{\mathfrak{N}}_{I})
.
The result now follows by Lemma
2.15
,
as each of
{}_{{\mathfrak{N}}_{I}}Y_{{\mathfrak{M}}}
and
{}_{{\mathfrak{N}}_{I}}{\mathfrak{M}}_{\mathfrak{M}}
lie in
{\mathcal{E}}\subset\mathsf{Bim}({\mathfrak{M}}\oplus{\mathfrak{N}}_{I})
.
∎

4.
Braided categorical nets

In
[
JNPW23
]
, an important role is played by the fusion categorical nets (or fusion spin chains) on
{\mathbb{Z}}
defined in Example
2.5
.
For higher dimensional lattices, extra structure is needed to define inclusion by tensoring with identity morphisms compatible with the geometric locality of the underlying lattice.
We now construct a canonical net of algebras associated to a choice of object
X
in a unitary
braided
fusion category
{\mathcal{B}}
.
We write
\beta_{a,b}:a\otimes b\to b\otimes a
for the braiding.
Our goal is to assign an object in
{\mathcal{B}}
to a finite rectangle in a
{\mathbb{Z}}^{2}
lattice, i.e.,

{\lxSVG@begingroup@{_scopebegin} \color[rgb]{0,0,1}\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces
\lxSVG@closescope }{{{{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces}}\lxSVG@begingroup@{_scopebegin} \lxSVG@transformcm{1.0}{0.0}{0.0}{1.0}{32.09373pt}{32.14929pt}\lxSVG@begingroup@{transform} \pgfsys@hbox{62}\lxSVG@closescope }}}

\lxSVG@closescope {\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces}{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces}{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces}\hss}\lxSVG@discardpath\lxSVG@closescope \hss}}\lxSVG@closescope\endpgfpicture}}}}\qquad\longmapsto\qquad{\mathfrak{A}}(\Lambda)=\End_{\mathcal{B}}(X^{\otimes\Lambda}).

In order to do so, we must make sense of the object
X^{\otimes\Lambda}\in{\mathcal{B}}
.
Our construction follows the idea sketched in
[
KJS+24
, §IV.B]
.
We do so in more generality, where we are allowed to assign any object to any site in
\Lambda
.
That is, if
b_{ij}\in{\mathcal{B}}
is the object assigned to site
(i,j)\in\Lambda
, we define
(b_{ij})^{\otimes\Lambda}
.

When
{\mathcal{B}}
is symmetric, there is an obvious choice for
(b_{ij})^{\otimes\Lambda}
, namely the
unordered tensor product
over the sites of
\Lambda
.
We choose an arbitrary ordering of the sites in
\Lambda
, say
(i_{n},j_{n})
, and we take the tensor product
\bigotimes_{n=1}^{N^{2}}b_{i_{n}j_{n}}\in{\mathcal{B}}

(here, we have assumed
\Lambda
has
N^{2}
sites).
Given another ordering
(i^{\prime}_{n},j^{\prime}_{n})
of the sites in
\Lambda
, there is a unique element
\sigma
of the symmetric group
S_{N^{2}}
which takes the first ordering to the second,
and we get a canonical unitary

u_{\sigma}:\bigotimes_{n=1}^{N^{2}}b_{i_{n}j_{n}}\to\bigotimes_{n=1}^{N^{2}}b_{i_{n}^{\prime}j_{n}^{\prime}}
.
Moreover, given any third ordering
(i^{\prime\prime}_{n},j^{\prime\prime}_{n})
,
there are canonical unitaries
\sigma^{\prime}
taking
(i^{\prime}_{n},j^{\prime}_{n})
to
(i^{\prime\prime}_{n},j^{\prime\prime}_{n})

and
\sigma^{\prime\prime}
taking

(i_{n},j_{n})
to
(i^{\prime\prime}_{n},j^{\prime\prime}_{n})
such that
\sigma^{\prime}\sigma=\sigma^{\prime\prime}
.
The corresponding canonical unitaries

u_{\sigma^{\prime}}:\bigotimes_{n=1}^{N^{2}}b_{i_{n}^{\prime}j_{n}^{\prime}}\to\bigotimes_{n=1}^{N^{2}}b_{i_{n}^{\prime\prime}j_{n}^{\prime\prime}}

and

u_{\sigma^{\prime\prime}}:\bigotimes_{n=1}^{N^{2}}b_{i_{n}j_{n}}\to\bigotimes_{n=1}^{N^{2}}b_{i_{n}^{\prime\prime}j_{n}^{\prime\prime}}

satisfy

u_{\sigma^{\prime}}u_{\sigma}=u_{\sigma^{\prime\prime}}
.
We thus have a contractible groupoid, and in this sense, the unordered tensor product
(b_{ij})^{\otimes\Lambda}
is canonical.

When
{\mathcal{B}}
is merely braided, we must be more careful.
We again proceed by choosing an arbitrary ordering
(i_{n},j_{n})
of the sites in
\Lambda
.
However, we now view this ordering as a interval
I
of sites on a
{\mathbb{Z}}
lattice contained in
{\mathbb{R}}^{2}
, and
our choice of ordering is replaced by

choice of homeomorphism of
{\mathbb{R}}^{2}
which moves sites
(i,j)\in\Lambda
to sites
I\subset{\mathbb{R}}^{2}
.
For example, we could choose a lexicographic ordering:

(4.1)

\Lambda

As above, we get an object
\bigotimes_{n=1}^{N^{2}}b_{i_{n}j_{n}}\in{\mathcal{B}}
.

Now for any two choices of homeomorphisms
h_{1},h_{2}
of
{\mathbb{R}}^{2}
which map
\Lambda\to I
, we get a canonical homeomorphism of the
N^{2}
-punctured plane by taking the punctures in
I
to themselves by

I\xrightarrow{h_{1}^{-1}}\Lambda\xrightarrow{h_{2}}I.

As the fundamental group of the
N^{2}
-punctured plane is the braid group
B_{N^{2}}
, this homeomorphism of
{\mathbb{R}}^{2}
which preserves
I
gives a canonical element
\beta_{12}\in B_{N^{2}}
, which gives a canonical unitary
u_{\beta_{12}}:\bigotimes_{n=1}^{N^{2}}b_{i_{n}j_{n}}\to\bigotimes_{n=1}^{N^{2}}b_{i_{n}^{\prime}j_{n}^{\prime}}
.
As before, for a third ordering, we get two more canonical elements of
B_{N^{2}}
and two more unitaries in
{\mathcal{B}}
which compose as they should.
We again get a contractible groupoid, and in this sense, the
braided tensor product

(b_{ij})^{\otimes\Lambda}
is canonical.

Remark 4.2
.

That the above object
(b_{i,j})^{\otimes\Lambda}
is well defined is proven carefully in

[
SW03
, Prop 7.6]
in the language of operads.
They work in the more restrictive setting that
{\mathcal{B}}
is
balanced
(although the authors of
[
SW03
]
use the term ribbon instead.)
A
balancing
structure is a unitary natural isomorphism
\theta:\id_{\mathcal{B}}\Rightarrow\id_{\mathcal{B}}
called the
twist
which satifies the balancing axiom

(\theta_{a}\otimes\theta_{b})\circ\beta_{b,a}\circ\beta_{a,b}=\theta_{a\otimes b}.

For example, if we equip
{\mathcal{B}}
with any unitary dual functor
\vee:{\mathcal{B}}\to{\mathcal{B}}^{\textrm{mop}}
in the sense of
[
Yam04
,
Sel11
,
Egg11
,
Pen20
]
,
3
3

3

Here
{\mathcal{B}}^{\textrm{mop}}
is the
monoidal opposite
category obtained by reversing the arrows of
{\mathcal{C}}
and also reversing the order of the tensor product.

the induced unitary pivotal structure is given by

\varphi_{b}:=(\coev_{b}^{\dagger}\otimes\id_{b^{\vee\vee}})\circ(\id_{b}\otimes\coev_{b^{\vee}})=(\id_{b^{\vee\vee}}\otimes\ev_{b})\circ(\ev_{b}^{\dagger}\otimes\id_{b})

which induces a canonical twist given by

This canonical twist induces a
ribbon structure
(that is,
\theta_{b^{\vee}}=\theta_{b}^{\vee}
)
if and only if
\varphi
is spherical
[
HPT16
, Appendix A.2]
.
In particular, we may choose to equip
{\mathcal{B}}
with its unique unitary spherical structure
[
LR97
]
; this is the only choice when
{\mathcal{B}}
is fusion
[
Pen20
]
.

In our setting, the balancing is not really needed as we are not keeping track of duality in defining
(b_{ij})^{\otimes\Lambda}
.

Now given a labeling
(b_{ij})
for sites
(i,j)\in\Lambda
and an inclusion
\Lambda\subset\Delta
, we get the labelling
(b_{ij})
for sites
(i,j)\in\Delta
by setting
b_{ij}:=1_{\mathcal{C}}
whenever
(i,j)\in\Delta\setminus\Lambda
.
We thus have a canonical isometry

(b_{ij})^{\otimes\Lambda}\to(b_{ij})^{\otimes\Delta}
which adds
1_{\mathcal{B}}
to all sites in
\Delta\setminus\Lambda
.
To see this is well-defined, pick an isotopy
\Delta\to I\cup J\subset{\mathbb{Z}}
where sites in
\Lambda
go to
I
, sites in
\Delta\setminus\Lambda
go to
J
, and
J
is to the right of
I
.
The map then corresponds to

\bigotimes_{n=1}^{N^{2}}b_{i_{n},j_{n}}\mapsto\bigotimes_{n=1}^{N^{2}}b_{i_{n},j_{n}}\otimes\bigotimes_{v\in J}1_{\mathcal{B}}
.

We now again fix an object
X\in{\mathcal{B}}
, and we consdider the map
\Lambda\mapsto{\mathfrak{A}}(\Lambda):=\End_{\mathcal{B}}(X^{\otimes\Lambda})
.
By choosing our isotopties as above, we see that
\Lambda\mapsto{\mathfrak{A}}(\Lambda)
indeed defines a net of algebras.

Definition 4.3

(Braided fusion categorical net)
.

Let
{\mathcal{B}}
be a braided fusion category with a choice of object
X\in{\mathcal{B}}
.
Consider the lattice
{\mathbb{Z}}^{2}
.
For a rectangle
\Lambda\subset{\mathbb{Z}}^{2}
, we define

{\mathfrak{A}}(\Lambda):=\End_{\mathcal{B}}(X^{\otimes\Lambda})

where

X^{\otimes\Lambda}
denotes the braided tensor product of copies of
X
over the points of
\Lambda
.

.

\lxSVG@closescope {\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces}{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces}{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces}\hss}\lxSVG@discardpath\lxSVG@closescope \hss}}\lxSVG@closescope\endpgfpicture}}}}:=({\color[rgb]{1,0,0}i_{X}^{\otimes\Lambda}})^{\dagger}\circ f\circ{\color[rgb]{1,0,0}i_{X}^{\otimes\Lambda}}\qquad\qquad\forall\,f\in{\mathfrak{A}}(\Lambda)=\End_{{\mathcal{B}}}({\color[rgb]{1,0,0}X^{\otimes\Lambda}})

where the red univalent vertex is the partial isometry
i_{X}:1_{{\mathcal{B}}}\hookrightarrow X

or its adjoint.
On the inductive limit algebra
{\mathfrak{A}}=\varinjlim{\mathfrak{A}}(\Lambda)
, we define the state
\psi:=\varinjlim\psi_{\Lambda}

(cf.
[
JNPW23
, Cor. 2.19]
).

We now consider the net
{\mathfrak{A}}
equipped with the state
\psi
, which results in a net of von Neumann algebras on the poset of cones in
{\mathbb{R}}^{2}
by taking
A_{\Lambda}:={\mathfrak{A}}(\Lambda)^{\prime\prime}
in the GNS representation of
\psi
.
We now prove that the net
A
satisfies Haag duality, and we compute the underlying
{\mathrm{W}}^{*}
-category of its superselection sectors.

Let
\langle X\rangle
denote the full braided fusion subcategory of
{\mathcal{B}}
generated by
X
and
\mathsf{Hilb}\langle X\rangle
its unitary ind completion
[
JP17
, §2.6]
(see also
[
NY16
]
).
Recall that the objects of
\mathsf{Hilb}\langle X\rangle
can be written as

\bigoplus_{x\in\Irr\langle X\rangle}H_{x}\otimes x

where
\Irr\langle X\rangle
denotes a set of representatives for the simple objects of
\langle X\rangle
, and each
H_{x}
is a separable (possibly infinite dimensional) multiplicity Hilbert space.

The following construction is the braided categorical net analog of
[
JNPW23
, Const. 6.13]
for fusion categorical nets.

Construction 4.4
.

x\in\Irr\langle X\rangle
.

For an arbitrary
z\in\mathsf{Hilb}\langle X\rangle
, we write
z=\bigoplus_{x\in\Irr\langle X\rangle}H_{x}\otimes x
and set
{\mathcal{K}}_{z}:=\bigoplus_{x\in\Irr\langle X\rangle}H_{x}\otimes{\mathcal{K}}_{x}
.

In fact, one can actually reduce the study of many structural properties of the 2D braided categorical net to the 1D setting, which have already been analyzed in detail in
[
Jon24
]
and
[
JNPW23
]
.
The main trick is that a cone splits the 2D plane into two halves, and the braiding can be used to move the
{\mathbb{Z}}^{2}
lattice points on either side of the split into a 1D
{\mathbb{Z}}
lattice.

\Lambda

We can thus infer properties about our braided categorical net
{\mathfrak{A}}
acting on
{\mathcal{K}}_{x}
from the fusion categorical setting.

For the results
Proposition
4.5
,
Lemma
4.6
,
and Theorem
4.7
below, our statments are given generally so that they may simultaneously be interpreted for 1D fusion spin systems and 2D braided fusion spin systems, and it suffices to prove the 1D case.
For the 1D case, we always take our cone
\Lambda
to be a 1-sided infinite interval in
{\mathbb{Z}}
, say
[1,\infty)
, and we set
\Lambda_{n}=[1,n]
so that
\Lambda=\bigcup\Lambda_{n}
.
(For 2D braided fusion spin systems,
\Lambda_{n}
should grow by more than 1 site at a time, corresponding to larger initial segments of the cone
\Lambda
.)
Without loss of generality, it then suffices to consider

{\mathcal{K}}_{x}(\Lambda_{n})={\mathcal{B}}(x\to X^{\otimes n}),

and
\Lambda_{n+1}
is obtained by adding sites to the right, so that the map
{\mathcal{K}}_{x}(\Lambda_{n})\hookrightarrow{\mathcal{K}}_{x}(\Lambda_{n+1})
is
-\otimes i_{X}
.

Proposition 4.5
.

Fix a cone
\Lambda
in
{\mathbb{R}}^{2}
.
If
x\in\langle X\rangle
, then the action of
{\mathfrak{A}}(\Lambda)
on
B({\mathcal{K}}_{x})
extends to a normal action of
A_{\Lambda}
.

Proof.

By
[
JP19
, Prop. 4.15 and Rem. 4.16(2)]
, it suffices to exhibit a dense subspace
{\mathcal{D}}_{x}\subset{\mathcal{K}}_{x}
whose vector states can be realized on
\bigcup{\mathfrak{A}}(\Lambda_{n})
by vectors in
{\mathcal{K}}_{1_{\mathcal{B}}}
.
Indeed, we claim
{\mathcal{D}}_{x}=\bigcup{\mathcal{K}}_{x}(\Delta)
works.
Since
x\in\langle X\rangle
, there is an isometry
v:x^{\vee}\to X^{\otimes n}
for some
n
.
Thus if
f\in{\mathcal{D}}_{x}
, we may add
n
sites to the
left
of those in
\Delta
to get
g:=(v\otimes f)\circ\ev^{\dagger}_{x}\in{\mathcal{K}}_{1_{\mathcal{B}}}
which realizes the vector state
\omega_{f}
.
For example, when
f\in{\mathcal{K}}_{x}(\Lambda_{n})
and
a\in{\mathfrak{A}}(\Lambda_{n})
, we have

\omega_{f}(a)=\tr_{\mathcal{B}}(f^{\dagger}af)=\vbox{\hbox{\hbox to58.48pt{\vbox to95.04pt{\pgfpicture\makeatletter\hbox{\hskip 45.07579pt\lower-47.51917pt\hbox to0.0pt{\lxSVG@begingroup@{_scopebegin} \lxSVG@begingroup@{stroke} \lxSVG@begingroup@{fill} \lxSVG@setlinewidth{\the\pgflinewidth}\lxSVG@begingroup@{stroke-width} \lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\nullfont\lxSVG@begingroup@{_scopebegin} \lxSVG@closescope \hbox to0.0pt{\lxSVG@begingroup@{_scopebegin}

Lemma 4.6
.

For a cone
\Lambda
, let
{\mathcal{K}}_{x}(\Lambda):=\varinjlim{\mathcal{K}}_{x}(\Lambda_{n})
for
\Lambda_{n}
bounded contractible regions which increase to
\Lambda
.
The action of
{\mathfrak{A}}(\Lambda)
on
{\mathcal{K}}_{x}(\Lambda)
is irreducible.

Proof.

Set
{\mathcal{L}}_{1}:={\mathcal{K}}_{x}(\Lambda_{1})
, and inductively define
{\mathcal{L}}_{n+1}:={\mathcal{K}}_{x}(\Lambda_{n+1})\ominus{\mathcal{K}}_{x}(\Lambda_{n})
.
Now
{\mathcal{K}}_{x}(\Lambda)=\bigoplus{\mathcal{L}}_{n}
, and we may choose an ONB
B_{n}
for each
{\mathcal{L}}_{n}
, and observe that the ONBs for
m\neq n
are orthogonal.
Moreover, for all
f,g\in B_{n}
, observe that

g^{\dagger}\circ f=\delta_{g=f}d_{x}^{-1}\cdot\id_{x}
.

We now observe that we can form a system of matrix units for the ONB
\bigcup B_{n}
of
{\mathcal{K}}_{x}(\Lambda)
which lie in
\bigcup{\mathfrak{A}}(\Lambda_{n})\subset{\mathfrak{A}}(\Lambda)
.
That is, for
f\in B_{m}
and
g\in B_{n}
with
m\leq n
, we define

e_{fg}:=\begin{cases}d_{x}\cdot(f\otimes i_{X}^{\otimes n-m})g^{\dagger}&\text{if }m<n\\
d_{x}\cdot fg^{\dagger}&\text{if }m=n\\
d_{x}\cdot f(g\otimes i_{X}^{\otimes m-n})^{\dagger}&\text{if }m>n,\end{cases}

which lies in
{\mathfrak{A}}(\Lambda_{\max\{m,n\}})
.
The result follows.
∎

Theorem 4.7
.

The net of von Neumann algebras
(A_{\Lambda})
satisfies Haag duality.
Moreover, each cone algebra
A_{\Lambda}
is a finite direct sums of type
\rm I_{\infty}
factors, with one summand for each simple object in the full fusion subcategory of
{\mathcal{B}}
generated by
X
.

Proof.

Consider
A_{\Lambda}
acting in the ground state representation

L^{2}({\mathfrak{A}},\psi)\cong{\mathcal{K}}_{1_{\mathcal{B}}}
.
Let
\Delta_{n}
be an increasing family of rectangles where
\bigcup\Delta_{n}
covers the entire lattice,
such that
\Delta_{n}\cap\Lambda=\Lambda_{n}
.
By semisimplicity,

\displaystyle{\mathcal{K}}_{x}(\Delta_{n})

\displaystyle={\mathcal{B}}(1_{\mathcal{C}}\to X^{\otimes\Delta_{n}})

\displaystyle\cong{\mathcal{B}}(\overline{X}^{\otimes\Delta_{n}\setminus\Lambda}\to X^{\otimes\Lambda_{n}})

\displaystyle\cong\bigoplus_{x\in\Irr\langle X\rangle}{\mathcal{B}}(\overline{X}^{\otimes\Delta\setminus\Lambda}\to x)\otimes{\mathcal{B}}(x\to X^{\otimes\Lambda_{n}})

\displaystyle=\bigoplus_{x\in\Irr\langle X\rangle}{\mathcal{B}}(\overline{X}^{\otimes\Delta_{n}\setminus\Lambda}\to x)\otimes{\mathcal{K}}_{x}(\Lambda_{n})

\displaystyle\cong\bigoplus_{x\in\Irr\langle X\rangle}{\mathcal{B}}(x^{\vee}\to X^{\otimes\Delta_{n}\setminus\Lambda})\otimes{\mathcal{K}}_{x}(\Lambda_{n})

\displaystyle\cong\bigoplus_{x\in\Irr\langle X\rangle}{\mathcal{K}}_{x^{\vee}}(\Delta_{n}\setminus\Lambda)\otimes{\mathcal{K}}_{x}(\Lambda_{n})

(There is a subtlety with the inner product on each summand above where one normalizes by
d_{X}
as in the proof of Lemma
4.6
, but this normalization does not affect the rest of this argument.)
One may visualize this isomorphism as splitting each map as follows.
