The
{\mathfrak{A}}(\Lambda_{n})
-action is by post-composition on the Hilbert space
{\mathcal{B}}(x\to X^{\otimes\Lambda_{n}})={\mathcal{K}}_{x}(\Lambda_{n})
,
and each space
{\mathcal{K}}_{x^{\vee}}(\Delta_{n}\setminus\Lambda)
acts as a multiplicity space for the
{\mathfrak{A}}(\Lambda_{n})
action.
Observe that the left
{\mathfrak{A}}(\Lambda_{n})
-action may never change the internal label
x\in\Irr\langle X\rangle
, and we thus see that
{\mathcal{K}}_{1_{\mathcal{B}}}
decomposes as an
{\mathfrak{A}}(\Lambda)
-representation as

\bigoplus_{x\in\Irr\langle X\rangle}{\mathcal{K}}_{x^{\vee}}(\Lambda^{c})\otimes{\mathcal{K}}_{x}(\Lambda).

We know that the action of
{\mathfrak{A}}(\Lambda)
on each
{\mathcal{K}}_{x}(\Lambda)
is irreducible, so
A_{\Lambda}\cong\bigoplus_{x\in\Irr\langle X\rangle}B({\mathcal{K}}_{x}(\Lambda))
is a finite direct sum of type
{\mathrm{I}}_{\infty}
factors as claimed.
The commutant is clearly the action by
{\mathfrak{A}}(\Lambda^{c})
on the multiplicity spaces.
∎

Thus our net of von Neumann algebras
(A_{\Lambda})
is isotone, properly infinite, and satisfies Haag duality.
By
[
BBC+24
, Thm. A]
, we have a well-defined braided
{\mathrm{W}}^{*}
-tensor category
\mathsf{SSS}(A)
of superselection sectors.
We now characterize the underlying
{\mathrm{W}}^{*}
-category of
\mathsf{SSS}(A)
.
Clearly the map
z\mapsto{\mathcal{K}}_{z}
is a unitary functor
\langle X\rangle^{\rm op}\to\mathsf{SSS}(A)
, as precomposition with
f\in{\mathcal{B}}(x\to y)
commutes with post-composition by
\End_{\mathcal{B}}(X^{\otimes\Lambda})
.

Theorem 4.8
.

The functor
\mathsf{Hilb}\langle X\rangle^{\rm op}\ni z\mapsto{\mathcal{K}}_{z}\in\mathsf{SSS}(A)
is a unitary equivalence of
{\mathrm{W}}^{*}
-categories.

Proof.

As with the above results, as we are ignoring the fusion and braiding, it suffices to consider the case of a 1D fusion spin system.
The result then follows by
[
JNPW23
, Const. 6.13 and Thm. 6.14]
(ignoring the module-action there, as we only care about the category itself).
∎

We leave the identification of the braiding and fusion of
\mathsf{SSS}(A)
with that of
\mathsf{Hilb}\langle X\rangle
to a future article.

4.2.
Bounded spread isomorphism to edge-restricted Levin-Wen operators

Notation 4.9
.

For a region
\Lambda
,
\Lambda^{+s}
is the smallest region containing all lattice points of distance at most
s
away from
\Lambda
.
When
\Lambda
is a rectangle,
\Lambda^{+s}
is another rectangle.
When
\Lambda
is a cone,
\Lambda^{+s}
means the cone obtained from
\Lambda
by moving the boundaries of the cone perpendicularly by
s
to obtain a larger cone.

Even though our
{\mathbb{Z}}^{n}
lattice is discrete, since
{\mathbb{Z}}^{n}\subset{\mathbb{R}}^{n}
, we say a region
\Lambda\subset{\mathcal{L}}
is
contractible
if the union of all edges and plaquettes contained in
\Lambda
is contractible in
{\mathbb{R}}^{n}
.

Definition 4.10
.

Suppose
{\mathfrak{A}}
and
{\mathfrak{B}}
are two nets of finite dimensional
\rm C^{*}
-algebras on the same lattice.
A
bounded spread isomorphism

\alpha:{\mathfrak{A}}\to{\mathfrak{B}}
is a
*
-algebra isomorphism between the quasi-local algebras such that there is a universal constant
s>0
called the
spread
such that
\alpha({\mathfrak{A}}(\Lambda))\subset{\mathfrak{B}}(\Lambda^{+s})

and

\alpha^{-1}({\mathfrak{B}}(\Lambda))\subset{\mathfrak{A}}(\Lambda^{+s})

for all bounded contractible
\Lambda
.

One utility of bounded spread isomorphism between nets of algebras is that bounded spread Haag duality for one net implies the same for the other
[
BBC+24
, Prop. 5.10]
in a given state.
Thus the two nets of algebras have isomorphic braided
{\mathrm{W}}^{*}
-tensor categories of superselection sectors
[
BBC+24
, Thm. C]
.

Example 4.11

(Intertwined nets of algebras)
.

Suppose
{\mathfrak{A}},{\mathfrak{B}}
are two nets of finite dimensional
{\mathrm{C}}^{*}
-algebras on the same lattice.
We say that
{\mathfrak{A}}
and
{\mathfrak{B}}
are
intertwined with spread
t>0
if
{\mathfrak{A}}(\Lambda)\subseteq{\mathfrak{B}}(\Lambda^{+t})
and
{\mathfrak{B}}(\Lambda)\subseteq{\mathfrak{A}}(\Lambda^{+t})
for all bounded contractible
\Lambda
.
Choosing increasing finite rectangles whose union is all of
{\mathcal{L}}
, we see that we have an
equality
of quasi-local algebras
{\mathfrak{A}}={\mathfrak{B}}
, and the identity map is manifestly bounded spread.

Sub-example 4.12

(
[
KJS+24
, § IV.E]
)
.

Consider the
edge restricted local Hilbert spaces
of the Levin-Wen model for a UFC
{\mathcal{C}}
given by
p^{A}_{\Lambda}\bigotimes_{v\in\Lambda}{\mathcal{H}}_{v}
where
p^{A}_{\Lambda}:=\prod_{\ell\in\Lambda}A_{\ell}
.
It was shown in
[
GHK+24
, Prop. 2.6]
that

p^{A}_{\Lambda}\bigotimes_{v\in\Lambda}{\mathcal{H}}_{v}\cong{\mathcal{C}}(X^{\partial\Lambda}\to F(A)^{\#p\in\Lambda})\cong Z({\mathcal{C}})(\Tr(X^{\partial\Lambda})\to A^{\#p\in\Lambda}),

where
X^{\partial\Lambda}
is the tensor product of our generator
X=\bigoplus_{c\in\Irr({\mathcal{C}})}c
over the number of edges in
\partial\Lambda
,
A\in Z({\mathcal{C}})
is the canonical Lagrangian algebra given by
A=I(1)
where
\Tr:{\mathcal{C}}\to Z({\mathcal{C}})
is the unitary adjoint
[
HPT24
, §2.1]
of the forgetful functor
F:Z({\mathcal{C}})\to{\mathcal{C}}
, and
\#p\in\Lambda
is the number of plaquettes in
\Lambda
.

We now consider two nets of algebras.
The first is given by

{\mathfrak{A}}(\Lambda):=\End_{Z({\mathcal{C}})}(A^{\#p\in\Lambda}),

which is exactly the commutant of

\End_{Z({\mathcal{C}})}(\Tr(X^{\otimes\partial\Lambda}))

on the above Hilbert space by Lemma
2.6
.
Indeed,
X
contains all simples in
{\mathcal{C}}
, so
\Tr(X^{\otimes\partial\Lambda})
contains all simples in
Z({\mathcal{C}})
.
It is worth mentioning that
\End_{Z({\mathcal{C}})}(\Tr(X^{\otimes\partial\Lambda}))
is Morita equivalent to Ocneanu’s tube algebra, which is given by

\bigoplus_{a,b,c\in\Irr({\mathcal{C}})}{\mathcal{C}}(ac\to cb)\cong\bigoplus_{a,b,c\in\Irr({\mathcal{C}})}{\mathcal{C}}(a\to cbc^{\vee})\cong{\mathcal{C}}(X\to F(\Tr(X))\cong\End_{Z({\mathcal{C}})}(\Tr(X)).

The action of
{\mathfrak{A}}(\Lambda)
is then by gluing a local operator in the braided categorical net for
Z({\mathcal{C}})
with strand label
A
(which is
not
a strong tensor generator!) onto these empty tubes.
The resulting diagram is again in
{\mathcal{C}}(X^{\partial\Lambda}\to F(A^{\#p\in\Lambda}))
.

Second, the
boundary preserving local operators

{\mathfrak{B}}(\Lambda)
are the endomorphisms of the local Hilbert spaces
\bigotimes_{v\in\Lambda}{\mathcal{H}}_{v}
which fix the labels on the external boundary edges of
\Lambda
.
Since operators in
{\mathfrak{A}}(\Lambda)
clearly fix the external boundary, we have an obvious inclusion

{\mathfrak{A}}(\Lambda)\subset{\mathfrak{B}}(\Lambda).

Note, however, that operators in
{\mathfrak{B}}(\Lambda)
need not preserve the internal edge labels.

Observe now that operators in
{\mathfrak{B}}(\Lambda)
included into
{\mathfrak{B}}(\Lambda^{+1})
commute with the external action of
\Tube_{\mathcal{C}}(\partial\Lambda^{+1})
!
Since

{\mathfrak{A}}(\Lambda^{+1})=\End_{\Tube_{\mathcal{C}}(\partial\Lambda^{+1})}({\mathcal{C}}(X^{\partial\Lambda^{+1}}\to F(A^{\#p\in\Lambda^{+1}})),

we see that
{\mathfrak{B}}(\Lambda)\subset{\mathfrak{A}}(\Lambda^{+1})
.
Thus the nets of algebra
{\mathfrak{A}},{\mathfrak{B}}
are intertwined.

In order to use the above intertwining to make a statement about an isomorphism of categories of superselection sectors, we must analyze the canonical states on
{\mathfrak{A}}
and
{\mathfrak{B}}
.
Recall that
\psi_{\mathfrak{A}}
on
{\mathfrak{A}}
from §
4.1
above is defined by conjugating by unit maps
1_{Z({\mathcal{C}})}\to A
for each site in
\Lambda
and taking inductive limits.
The state
\psi_{\mathfrak{B}}
is given on
{\mathfrak{B}}(\Lambda)
by compressing by
p_{\Delta}
for
\Lambda\Subset_{1}\Delta
as in §
2.2
:

\psi_{\mathfrak{B}}(x)p_{\Delta}=p_{\Delta}xp_{\Delta}\qquad\qquad\qquad\forall\,x\in{\mathfrak{B}}(\Lambda).

Observe that for the image of
{\mathfrak{A}}(\Lambda)\subset{\mathfrak{B}}(\Lambda)
, compressing by
p_{\Delta}
implements the conjugation by the unit maps by
[
GHK+24
, Rem. 2.10]
.
In more detail, in the graphical calculus of strings on tubes for the categorified trace from
[
HPT16
]
, we have

Thus compressing an operator
f\in{\mathfrak{A}}(\Lambda)
by
p_{\Delta}
gives

p_{\Delta}xp_{\Delta}=\psi_{\mathfrak{A}}(x)p_{\Delta},

which implies
\psi_{\mathfrak{B}}(f)=\psi_{\mathfrak{A}}(f)
.
We thus see that
\psi_{\mathfrak{A}}=\psi_{\mathfrak{B}}
on the inductive limit algebras
{\mathfrak{A}},{\mathfrak{B}}
.

As
{\mathfrak{A}},{\mathfrak{B}}
are intertwined and
{\mathfrak{A}}
satisfies Haag duality in the state
\psi
by Theorem
4.7
,
{\mathfrak{B}}
satisfies bounded spread Haag duality in the state
\psi
by
[
BBC+24
, Prop. 5.10]
.
Thus
{\mathfrak{B}}
has a well-defined braided
{\mathrm{W}}^{*}
-tensor category of superselection sectors by
[
Oga22
]
or
[
BBC+24
, Thm. B]
.
By
[
BBC+24
, Thm. C]
, the braided
{\mathrm{W}}^{*}
-tensor categories of superselection sectors for
{\mathfrak{B}}
and
{\mathfrak{A}}
are isomorphic.
By Theorem
4.8
, the underlying
{\mathrm{W}}^{*}
-category of the superselection sectors for
{\mathfrak{A}}
is equivalent to the full subcategory of
\mathsf{Hilb}(Z({\mathcal{C}}))
generated by
A
, i.e.,
\mathsf{Hilb}\langle A\rangle
.
We thus have the following theorem.

Theorem 4.13
.

The superselection sector category for the net of boundary preserving local operators in the Levin-Wen model is equivalent to
\mathsf{Hilb}\langle A\rangle\subset\mathsf{Hilb}(Z({\mathcal{C}}))
, the full subcategory generated by the canonical Lagrangian algebra
A=\Tr(1)
.

Remark 4.14
.

Note that the above theorem only establishes an isomorphism of
{\mathrm{W}}^{*}
-categories, and not braided
{\mathrm{W}}^{*}
-tensor categories, as we have not yet identified composition of superselection sectors for the braided categorical net with the tensor product and braiding in
\mathsf{Hilb}(Z({\mathcal{C}}))
.

4.3.
Adapting the Levin-Wen model to see all excitations in the edge-restricted sector

Unfortunately, only the fluxes (summands of the canonical Lagrangian algebra) appear as superselection sectors in Theorem
4.13
above.
The model from
[
GHK+24
, Rem. 3.5]
due to the first author is a generalization of the Levin-Wen model where we can see charges and dyons as superselection sectors of the net of boundary preserving local algebras, and not just fluxes.

There is also a
unit term
local projector
C_{v}
for each vertex
v
which only allows
z=1_{Z({\mathcal{C}})}
at
v
.
Thus the local Hamiltonian

H=-\sum A_{\ell}-\sum B_{p}-\sum C_{v}

again recovers the
{\mathcal{C}}
-skein module as its ground state space.

We now proceed as in Sub-Example
4.12
with our augmented Levin-Wen model.
We pass to the edge restricted local Hilbert spaces
p^{A}_{\Lambda}\bigotimes_{v\in\Lambda}{\mathcal{H}}_{v}
where
p^{A}_{\Lambda}:=\prod_{\ell\subset\Lambda}A_{\ell}
.
By an argument similar to
[
GHK+24
, Prop. 2.6]
,

p^{A}_{\Lambda}\bigotimes_{v\in\Lambda}{\mathcal{H}}_{v}={\mathcal{C}}(X^{\partial\Lambda}\to F(A)^{\#p\in\Lambda}\otimes F(Y)^{\#v\in\Lambda})\cong Z({\mathcal{C}})(\Tr(X^{\partial\Lambda})\to A^{\#p\in\Lambda}\otimes Y^{\#v\in\Lambda})

where again
F:Z({\mathcal{C}})\to{\mathcal{C}}
is the forgetful functor,
\Tr:{\mathcal{C}}\to Z({\mathcal{C}})
is its unitary adjoint,

A=\Tr(1)
is the canonical Lagrangian algebra,

X=\bigoplus_{c\in\Irr({\mathcal{C}})}c
, and

Y=\bigoplus_{z\in\Irr(Z({\mathcal{C}}))}z
.
Using a similar intertwining argument, the boundary preserving local operators
{\mathfrak{B}}(\Lambda)
contains

{\mathfrak{A}}(\Lambda):=\End_{\Tube_{\mathcal{C}}(\partial\Lambda)}(Z({\mathcal{C}})(\Tr(X^{\partial\Lambda})\to A^{\#p\in\Lambda}\otimes Y^{\#v\in\Lambda}))=\End_{Z({\mathcal{C}})}(A^{\#p\in\Lambda}\otimes Y^{\#v\in\Lambda}),

and
{\mathfrak{B}}(\Lambda)\subset{\mathfrak{A}}(\Lambda^{+1})
as before.
One can view the net of algebras
{\mathfrak{A}}
as a braided fusion categorical net built from
two generators
{\color[rgb]{0,1,1}A=\Tr(1)}
and
{\color[rgb]{1,0,0}Y=\bigoplus_{z\in\Irr(Z({\mathcal{C}})}z}

on a 2D edge lattice.

{}{}}
{{}{{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces}}}{{}{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces}}{}{{}{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces}}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces
}{{{{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces}}\lxSVG@begingroup@{_scopebegin} \lxSVG@transformcm{1.0}{0.0}{0.0}{1.0}{25.46663pt}{11.72638pt}\lxSVG@begingroup@{transform} \pgfsys@hbox{62}\lxSVG@closescope }}}
\lxSVG@closescope }}}
\lxSVG@closescope {\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces}{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces}{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces}\hss}\lxSVG@discardpath\lxSVG@closescope \hss}}\lxSVG@closescope\endpgfpicture}}}}:=({\color[rgb]{0,1,1}i_{A}^{\#p\in\Lambda}}\otimes{\color[rgb]{1,0,0}i_{Y}^{\#v\in\Lambda}})^{\dagger}\circ f\circ({\color[rgb]{0,1,1}i_{A}^{\#p\in\Lambda}}\otimes{\color[rgb]{1,0,0}i_{Y}^{\#v\in\Lambda}})\quad\forall\,f\in\End_{Z({\mathcal{C}})}({\color[rgb]{0,1,1}A^{\#p\in\Lambda}}\otimes{\color[rgb]{1,0,0}Y^{\#v\in\Lambda}}).

Here, the
cyan univalent vertex is the partial isometry
i_{A}:1_{Z({\mathcal{C}})}\hookrightarrow A

or its adjoint, and the
red univalent vertex is the partial isometry
i_{Y}:1_{Z({\mathcal{C}})}\hookrightarrow Y

or its adjoint.
Indeed,
\psi(f)p_{\Delta}=p_{\Delta}fp_{\Delta}
for all
\Lambda\ll\Delta
,
and
compression of
f
by

p_{\Delta}=p^{B}_{\Delta}p^{C}_{\Delta}
is easily seen to conjugate
f
by both

{\color[rgb]{0,1,1}i_{A}^{\#p\in\Lambda}}

and

{\color[rgb]{1,0,0}i_{Y}^{\#v\in\Lambda}}

where appropriate,
corresponding to the compression of
f

of both
p^{C}_{\Delta}
and
p^{B}_{\Delta}
respectively.

As the nets
{\mathfrak{A}},{\mathfrak{B}}
are intertwined, they yield isomorphic
{\mathrm{W}}^{*}
-tensor categories of superselection sectors after completing the cone von Neumann algebras in the GNS representation of the canonical ground state
\psi
.
Since
\mathsf{Hilb}\langle A\otimes Y\rangle=\mathsf{Hilb}(Z({\mathcal{C}}))
, we have the following theorem.

Theorem 4.15
.

The superselection sector category for the net of boundary preserving local operators in the augmented Levin-Wen model is equivalent to
\mathsf{Hilb}(Z({\mathcal{C}}))
.

We conclude that we can now see all excitations and not just those under
A\in Z({\mathcal{C}})
.

4.4.
Braided-enriched fusion categorical net on a lattice with boundary

In §
3.1
above, we saw how to construct a fusion module spin chain
{\mathfrak{M}}
from a module category
{\mathcal{M}}_{\mathcal{C}}
for a fusion category
{\mathcal{C}}
on a 1D
{\mathbb{Z}}
lattice with boundary.
On a 2D
{\mathbb{Z}}^{2}
lattice with a 1D
{\mathbb{Z}}
boundary, we can use a
braided-enriched
fusion category to construct a braided fusion module categorical net.

Braided-enriched fusion categories were introduced in
[
MP19
]
and shown to be equivalent to
module fusion categories

[
HPT16
,
KZ18a
]
over a braided fusion category.
In more detail, given a unitary braided fusion category
{\mathcal{A}}
, a unitary
module fusion category
for
{\mathcal{A}}
or a
unitary
{\mathcal{A}}
-enriched fusion category
is a unitary fusion category
{\mathcal{X}}
equipped with a unitary braided central functor
\Phi^{Z}:{\mathcal{A}}\to Z({\mathcal{X}})
.
This central functor is exactly the data needed to hook up the 3D Walker-Wang model for
{\mathcal{A}}

[
WW12
]
to the 2D Levin-Wen model for
{\mathcal{X}}

[
LW05
]
as discussed in
[
HBJP23
,
GHK+24
]
.
We will discuss this lattice model in more detail in §
5
below.

Just as one can assign a well-defined object
(a_{ij})^{\otimes\Lambda}\in{\mathcal{A}}
to a tuple of objects
a_{ij}\in{\mathcal{A}}
for
(i,j)\in\Lambda
,
we can assign an object
(x_{ij})^{\otimes\Lambda}\in{\mathcal{X}}
to a tuple of objects
x_{ij}\in{\mathcal{X}}
indexed by a subset
(i,j)\in\Lambda
as long as
\Lambda
meets the boundary
\partial{\mathcal{L}}
of our
{\mathbb{Z}}^{2}
lattice, and
x_{ij}\in Z({\mathcal{X}})
for all sites
(i,j)
which do not lie in the boundary
\partial{\mathcal{L}}
, i.e.,
(i,j)\in\Lambda\setminus\partial{\mathcal{L}}
.

\Lambda
\partial{\mathcal{L}}

That is, the lattice sites colored black belonging to
\Lambda\cap\partial{\mathcal{L}}
above are assigned objects
x_{ij}\in{\mathcal{X}}
and the lattice sites colored red belonging to
\Lambda\setminus\partial{\mathcal{L}}
above are assigned objects
x_{ij}\in Z({\mathcal{X}})
.
As we assumed
{\mathcal{X}}
is
{\mathcal{A}}
-enriched so that we have a braided central functor
\Phi^{Z}:{\mathcal{A}}\to Z({\mathcal{X}})
, we can label sites colored black belonging to
\Lambda\cap\partial{\mathcal{L}}
by objects
x_{ij}\in{\mathcal{X}}
and lattice cites colored red belonging to
\Lambda\setminus\partial{\mathcal{L}}
by objects
a_{ij}\in{\mathcal{A}}
.
As the objects
\Phi^{Z}(a_{ij})\in Z({\mathcal{X}})
, we thus get a well-defined object

(x_{ij})^{\otimes\Lambda\cap\partial{\mathcal{L}}}\lhd(a_{ij})^{\otimes\Lambda\setminus\partial{\mathcal{L}}}=(x_{ij})^{\otimes\Lambda\cap\partial{\mathcal{L}}}\otimes(\Phi^{Z}(a_{ij}))^{\otimes\Lambda\setminus\partial{\mathcal{L}}}.

Here, we have implicitly chosen a lexicographic ordering of the sites in
\Lambda
as in (
4.1
), as the
x_{ij}\in{\mathcal{X}}
are only linearly ordered along
\partial{\mathcal{L}}
, so that the
\Phi^{Z}(a_{ij})
appear to the right, viewing
{\mathcal{X}}
as a right
{\mathcal{A}}
-module (tensor) category.

Definition 4.16

(Braided-enriched fusion categorical net)
.

Let
{\mathcal{A}}
be a braided unitary fusion category and let
{\mathcal{X}}
be an
{\mathcal{A}}
-enriched unitary fusion category, i.e.,
{\mathcal{X}}
is a unitary fusion category equipped with a braided unitary tensor functor
\Phi^{Z}:{\mathcal{A}}\to Z({\mathcal{X}})
.
We write
\Phi:=\Forget\circ\Phi^{Z}:{\mathcal{A}}\to{\mathcal{X}}
.
Let
A\in{\mathcal{A}}
and
X\in{\mathcal{X}}
be a
strongly generating pair
, i.e., there are
n,k\in{\mathbb{N}}
such that every simple object of
{\mathcal{X}}
appears as a direct summand of

X^{\otimes n}\lhd A^{\otimes k}=X^{\otimes n}\otimes\Phi^{Z}(A)^{\otimes k}.

For example, we may take
X=\bigoplus_{x\in\Irr({\mathcal{X}})}x
and
A=\bigoplus_{a\in\Irr({\mathcal{A}})}a
.
For rectangles
\Lambda
which do not meet
\partial{\mathcal{L}}
, we assign the algebra
{\mathfrak{X}}(\Lambda)
to be the value of the braided categorical net that
({\mathcal{A}},A)
would assign to
\Lambda
, i.e.,
{\mathfrak{X}}(\Lambda):=\End_{\mathcal{A}}(A^{\otimes\Lambda})
.
For rectangles
\Delta
which meet
\partial{\mathcal{L}}
, we assign

{\mathfrak{X}}(\Delta)=\End_{\mathcal{X}}(X^{\otimes\Delta\cap\partial{\mathcal{L}}}\lhd A^{\otimes\Delta\setminus\partial{\mathcal{L}}})
.

{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces
}{{{{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces}}\lxSVG@begingroup@{_scopebegin} \lxSVG@transformcm{1.0}{0.0}{0.0}{1.0}{79.57875pt}{-3.47221pt}\lxSVG@begingroup@{transform} \pgfsys@hbox{62}\lxSVG@closescope }}}

\lxSVG@closescope {\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces}{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces}{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces}\hss}\lxSVG@discardpath\lxSVG@closescope \hss}}\lxSVG@closescope\endpgfpicture}}}}\qquad\qquad\begin{aligned} \Lambda&\longmapsto{\mathfrak{X}}(\Lambda)=\End_{\mathcal{A}}(A^{\otimes\Lambda})\\
\Delta&\longmapsto{\mathfrak{X}}(\Delta)=\End_{\mathcal{X}}(X^{\otimes\Delta\cap\partial{\mathcal{L}}}\lhd A^{\otimes\Delta\setminus\partial{\mathcal{L}}})\end{aligned}

One uses the braided central functor
\Phi^{Z}
to obtain the inclusion
{\mathfrak{X}}(\Lambda)\subset{\mathfrak{X}}(\Delta)
for such regions.
One checks that
{\mathfrak{X}}
is a net of algebras on the
{\mathbb{Z}}^{2}
lattice with
{\mathbb{Z}}
boundary.

To compute the tensor category of DHR bimodules, we use the folding trick.
Given a boundary rectangle
\Delta
meeting
\partial{\mathcal{L}}
,
we fold our lattice
{\mathcal{L}}
with boundary into a thickened 1D lattice with boundary, which we call a ‘1D slab’.
This process squeezes the bulk lattice sites of
\Delta
farther into the center of this thickened 1D slab, but choosing a careful bijection
{\mathbb{Z}}\times{\mathbb{N}}\to{\mathbb{N}}
, we can view
\Delta
as sitting inside a boundary interval of the 1D slab.

\partial{\mathcal{L}}
\cdots

This process allows us to perform a dimensional reduction to consider our 2D net of algebras
{\mathfrak{X}}
with boundary as a 1D net of algebras
{\mathfrak{M}}
with boundary.
Here, we use
{\mathfrak{M}}
for the 1D boundary net as the situation is completely analogous to the boundary Levin-Wen setup from §
3.1
.

We now observe that any boundary DHR bimodule in
\mathsf{DHR}^{\partial}({\mathfrak{X}})
can be viewed as a boundary DHR bimodule in
\mathsf{DHR}^{\partial}({\mathfrak{M}})
.
We can now identify
{\mathfrak{M}}
with a fusion module categorical net as in (
3.7
).
The single boundary site on the left in the 1D slab corresponds to
{\mathcal{M}}={\mathcal{X}}
as a right module for the unitary multifusion category

{\mathcal{C}}={\mathcal{X}}^{\rm mp}\boxtimes_{\mathcal{A}}{\mathcal{A}}\boxtimes_{\mathcal{A}}{\mathcal{X}}\cong{\mathcal{X}}^{\rm mp}\boxtimes_{\mathcal{A}}{\mathcal{X}}.

Here, we use the
ladder category model
for the Deligne product
[
Row19
,
BBJ19
]
.
In more detail
{\mathcal{X}}^{\rm mp}\boxtimes_{\mathcal{A}}{\mathcal{X}}
is the unitary multifusion category obtained by taking the unitary Cauchy completion
[
GMP+23
, §3.1.1]
of
{\mathcal{L}}=\mathsf{Lad}({\mathcal{X}}^{\rm mp},{\mathcal{A}},{\mathcal{X}})
; the latter has has objects formal symbols
x^{\rm mp}\boxtimes y
for
x,y\in{\mathcal{X}}
and

\Hom(x_{1}^{\rm mp}\boxtimes y_{1}\to x_{2}^{\rm mp}\boxtimes y_{2}):=\bigoplus_{a\in\Irr({\mathcal{A}})}{\mathcal{X}}^{\rm mp}(x_{1}^{\rm mp}\to x_{2}^{\rm mp}\lhd a)\otimes{\mathcal{X}}(a\rhd y_{1}\to y_{2})

where
x^{\rm mp}\lhd a:=x^{\rm mp}\otimes_{{\mathcal{X}}^{\rm mp}}\Phi(a)^{\rm mp}=(\Phi(a)\otimes x)^{\rm mp}

and
a\rhd x:=\Phi(a)\otimes x
is the
{\mathcal{A}}
-action on
{\mathcal{X}}
via
\Phi:=\Forget\circ\Phi^{Z}:{\mathcal{A}}\to{\mathcal{X}}
.
To compose morphisms, we stack ladders vertically and decompose the rungs into simples using the semisimplicity relation for
{\mathcal{A}}
.

Tensor product on objects is given by

(x^{\rm mp}\boxtimes y)\otimes_{\mathcal{L}}(w^{\rm mp}\boxtimes z):=(x^{\rm mp}\otimes_{{\mathcal{X}}^{\rm mp}}w^{\rm mp})\boxtimes(y\otimes_{\mathcal{X}}z)=(w\otimes_{\mathcal{X}}x)^{\rm mp}\boxtimes(y\otimes_{\mathcal{X}}z),

and on morphisms, it is nesting ladders using that the
{\mathcal{A}}
-action factors through
{\mathcal{A}}\to Z({\mathcal{X}})
.
4
4

4

It appears that our ‘nested’ monoidal product differs from the one defined in
[
Row19
, §3.2.1]
, but this is a manifestation of the fact that one copy of
{\mathcal{X}}
has the opposite monoidal product.

In our model,
{\mathcal{M}}={\mathcal{X}}
and
{\mathcal{C}}={\mathcal{X}}\boxtimes_{\mathcal{A}}{\mathcal{A}}\boxtimes_{\mathcal{A}}{\mathcal{X}}^{\rm mp}
which means our ladders really have 3 vertical strands and two horizontal rungs, but this is not important.
The generators for
{\mathcal{M}}
and
{\mathcal{C}}
in our model are

W:=\bigoplus_{z\in\Irr({\mathcal{X}})}z\qquad\qquad\qquad X:=\bigoplus_{\begin{subarray}{c}x,y\in\Irr({\mathcal{X}})\\
a\in\Irr({\mathcal{A}})\end{subarray}}x^{\rm mp}\boxtimes a\boxtimes y

respectively.
Even though
{\mathcal{C}}
is now multifusion, Construction
3.9
applies; it is for this reason that Appendix
A
is written in this generality (see Remark
3.11
).
Hence for each
F\in\End({\mathcal{M}}_{\mathcal{C}})
, we get a boundary DHR bimodule
{}_{\mathfrak{M}}Y^{F}_{\mathfrak{M}}\in\mathsf{DHR}^{\partial}({\mathfrak{M}})
.
By Theorem
3.14
, we conclude that

\mathsf{DHR}^{\partial}({\mathfrak{M}})\cong\End({\mathcal{M}}_{\mathcal{C}})
as unitary tensor categories.
Now as

{\mathcal{C}}={\mathcal{X}}^{\rm mp}\boxtimes_{\mathcal{A}}{\mathcal{A}}\boxtimes_{\mathcal{A}}{\mathcal{X}}\cong{\mathcal{X}}^{\rm mp}\boxtimes_{\mathcal{A}}{\mathcal{X}}

as multifusion categories, by

[
HBJP23
, Ex. II.9]

together with the folding trick in the 4-category of unitary braided fusion categories
[
BJS21
]
,
5
5

5

Braided fusion categories are fully dualizable in the 4-category of braided tensor categories by
[
BJS21
]
, which allows us to apply the folding trick.

we have

\End({\mathcal{M}}_{\mathcal{C}})\cong\End({\mathcal{X}}_{{\mathcal{X}}^{\rm mp}\boxtimes_{\mathcal{A}}{\mathcal{X}}})\cong\End^{\mathcal{A}}({}_{\mathcal{X}}{\mathcal{X}}_{{\mathcal{X}}})\cong Z^{\mathcal{A}}({\mathcal{X}})={\mathcal{A}}^{\prime}\subset Z({\mathcal{X}}),

the
enriched center
of
{\mathcal{X}}
as an
{\mathcal{A}}
-enriched fusion category
[
KZ18b
]
, a.k.a., the
Müger centralizer
of
{\mathcal{A}}\subset Z({\mathcal{X}})

[
Müg03
]
.
Here,
\End^{\mathcal{A}}({}_{\mathcal{X}}{\mathcal{X}}_{\mathcal{X}})
denotes the the
{\mathcal{A}}
-enriched endomorphisms in the 3-category of
{\mathcal{A}}
-enriched unitary fusion categories.

Proposition 4.19
.

The unitary tensor category of boundary DHR bimodules
\mathsf{DHR}^{\partial}({\mathfrak{X}})
is equivalent to the enriched center
Z^{\mathcal{A}}({\mathcal{X}})
.

With this proposition in hand, we can give a 2D construction of each boundary DHR bimodule
Y^{z}
for
z\in Z^{\mathcal{A}}({\mathcal{X}})
parallel to the 1D Construction
3.9
which exhausts all boundary DHR bimodules.
Pick an initial boundary point
\lambda_{0}\in\partial{\mathcal{L}}
, and inductively construct a sequence of rectangles by

\Lambda_{0}:=\{\lambda_{0}\}
and
\Lambda_{n+1}=\Lambda_{n}^{+1}
, i.e.,
\Lambda_{n}^{+1}
is obtained from
\Lambda_{n}
by adding all points in
{\mathcal{L}}
with
\ell^{1}
-distance 1.
For
n\in{\mathbb{N}}
, we define

Y^{z}_{n}:=\Hom_{\mathcal{X}}(X^{\otimes\Lambda_{n}\cap\partial{\mathcal{L}}}\lhd A^{\otimes\Lambda_{n}\setminus\partial{\mathcal{L}}}\to X^{\otimes\Lambda_{n}\cap\partial{\mathcal{L}}}\lhd A^{\otimes\Lambda_{n}\setminus\partial{\mathcal{L}}}\otimes z).

The inclusion
Y_{n}^{z}\hookrightarrow Y^{z}_{n+1}
is achieved by tensoring with identity morphisms,
\id_{X}
for sites in
\partial{\mathcal{L}}
and
\id_{A}
for sites in
{\mathcal{L}}\setminus\partial{\mathcal{L}}
.
One uses the braiding in
Z({\mathcal{X}})
to move the
z
-string past the
\id_{A}
-strings, and since
z\in Z^{\mathcal{A}}({\mathcal{X}})
, the inclusion is independent of the choice of how one performs this braiding.

\lxSVG@closescope {\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces}{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces}{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces}\hss}\lxSVG@discardpath\lxSVG@closescope \hss}}\lxSVG@closescope\endpgfpicture}}}}\in Y^{z}_{4}.

Here, we use the convention from
[
GHK+24
, Rem. 2.12]
; even though stands corresponding to
A\in{\mathcal{A}}
go upwards, the
z
-strand in the centralizer
Z^{\mathcal{A}}({\mathcal{X}})={\mathcal{A}}^{\prime}\subset Z({\mathcal{X}})
is drawn on the other side of
{\mathcal{X}}
to emphasize that
{\mathcal{X}}
is an
{\mathcal{A}}-Z^{\mathcal{A}}({\mathcal{X}})
bimodule tensor category.
The
Y^{z}_{n}
are equipped with the obvious
{\mathfrak{X}}(\Lambda_{n})
-valued inner products which are compatible with the inclusion maps.
We thus obtain a well-defined inductive limit bimodule
Y^{z}:=\varinjlim Y^{z}_{n}
which clearly lies in
\mathsf{DHR}^{\partial}({\mathfrak{X}})
.
The bimodules
Y^{z}
assemble into a functor
Y:Z^{\mathcal{A}}({\mathcal{X}})\to\mathsf{DHR}^{\partial}({\mathfrak{X}})
which is fully faithful by the argument from Appendix
A
.
Indeed, this is shown at the level of the 1D fusion module categorical nets for the 1D slab.

Now since the 1D fusion module categorical net satisfies boundary algebraic Haag duality by (
3.13
) (see also Appendix
A
), the 2D enriched fusion category categorical net satisfies boundary algebraic Haag duality.
This allows us to follow the prescription from
[
Jon24
]
to define a unitary braiding on the boundary DHR bimodules
\mathsf{DHR}^{\partial}({\mathfrak{X}})
.

Definition 4.20
.

Suppose
Y,Z\in\mathsf{DHR}^{\partial}({\mathfrak{X}})
.
Choose projective bases
\{b_{i}\},\{c_{j}\}
for
Y,Z
respectively which are localized in sufficiently large rectangles
\Lambda,\Delta
which are sufficiently far apart in
{\mathcal{L}}
, both of which meet
\partial{\mathcal{L}}
.
We define

u^{\Lambda,\Delta}_{Y,Z}:Y\boxtimes_{\mathfrak{X}}Z\rightarrow Z\boxtimes_{\mathfrak{X}}Y\qquad\qquad\text{by}\qquad\qquad\sum_{i,j}b_{i}\boxtimes c_{j}a_{ij}\mapsto\sum_{i,j}c_{j}\boxtimes b_{i}a_{ij}.

As in
[
Jon24
, §3.3]
,
one verifies this formula is a well-defined unitary
{\mathfrak{X}}-{\mathfrak{X}}
bimodule map which is independent of the choices of
\Lambda,\Delta
, provided they are sufficiently large and separated, and also independent of the choices of projective bases.
(Observe that the previous subtlety in 1D is no longer relevant thanks to the boundary.)

We provide some initial details to convince the reader that this works as claimed.
In all the calculations below, the elements with underbraces live in the indicated algebras by Lemma
2.23
.
First, for all
a_{ij}\in{\mathfrak{X}}
,

\displaystyle\left\langle u_{Y,Z}^{\Lambda,\Delta}\sum b_{i}\boxtimes c_{j}a_{ij}\bigg|u_{Y,Z}^{\Lambda,\Delta}\sum b_{k}\boxtimes c_{\ell}a_{k\ell}\right\rangle

\displaystyle=\sum a_{ij}^{*}\langle c_{j}\boxtimes b_{i}|c_{\ell}\boxtimes b_{k}\rangle_{{\mathfrak{X}}}a_{k\ell}

\displaystyle=\sum a_{ij}^{*}\langle b_{i}|\underbrace{\langle c_{j}|c_{\ell}\rangle_{{\mathfrak{X}}}}_{\in{\mathfrak{X}}(\Delta)}b_{k}\rangle_{{\mathfrak{X}}}a_{k\ell}

\displaystyle=\sum a_{ij}^{*}\langle b_{i}|b_{k}\langle c_{j}|c_{\ell}\rangle_{{\mathfrak{X}}}\rangle a_{k\ell}

\displaystyle=\sum a_{ij}^{*}\underbrace{\langle b_{i}|b_{k}\rangle_{\mathfrak{X}}}_{\in{\mathfrak{X}}(\Lambda)}\langle c_{j}|c_{\ell}\rangle_{{\mathfrak{X}}}a_{k\ell}

\displaystyle=\sum a_{ij}^{*}\langle c_{j}|c_{\ell}\rangle_{{\mathfrak{X}}}\langle b_{i}|b_{k}\rangle_{\mathfrak{X}}a_{k\ell}

\displaystyle=\sum a_{ij}^{*}\langle c_{j}|c_{\ell}\langle b_{i}|b_{k}\rangle_{\mathfrak{X}}\rangle_{{\mathfrak{X}}}a_{k\ell}

\displaystyle=\sum a_{ij}^{*}\langle c_{j}|\langle b_{i}|b_{k}\rangle_{\mathfrak{X}}c_{\ell}\rangle_{{\mathfrak{X}}}a_{k\ell}

\displaystyle=\sum a_{ij}^{*}\langle b_{i}\boxtimes c_{j}|b_{k}\boxtimes c_{\ell}\rangle_{\mathfrak{X}}a_{k\ell}

\displaystyle=\left\langle\sum b_{i}\boxtimes c_{j}a_{ij}\bigg|\sum b_{k}\boxtimes c_{\ell}a_{k\ell}\right\rangle.

This map is manifestly a right
{\mathfrak{X}}
-module map.
To see left
{\mathfrak{X}}
-linearity, we calculate

\displaystyle u^{\Lambda,\Delta}_{Y,Z}(ab_{k}\boxtimes c_{j})

\displaystyle=u^{\Lambda,\Delta}_{Y,Z}\sum b_{i}\underbrace{\langle b_{i}|ab_{k}\rangle_{\mathfrak{X}}}_{\in{\mathfrak{X}}(\Lambda)}\boxtimes c_{j}

\displaystyle=u^{\Lambda,\Delta}_{Y,Z}\sum b_{i}\boxtimes\langle b_{i}|ab_{k}\rangle_{\mathfrak{X}}c_{j}

\displaystyle=u^{\Lambda,\Delta}_{Y,Z}\sum b_{i}\boxtimes c_{j}\langle b_{i}|ab_{k}\rangle_{\mathfrak{X}}

\displaystyle=\sum c_{j}\boxtimes b_{i}\langle b_{i}|ab_{k}\rangle_{\mathfrak{X}}

\displaystyle=c_{j}\boxtimes ab_{k}

\displaystyle=c_{j}a\boxtimes b_{k}

\displaystyle=ac_{j}\boxtimes b_{k}

\displaystyle=au^{\Lambda,\Delta}_{Y,Z}(b_{k}\boxtimes c_{j}).

If
\{b_{k}^{\prime}\}
,
\{c_{\ell}^{\prime}\}
are another choice of bases still localized in
\Lambda,\Delta
respectively, we have

\displaystyle u^{\Lambda,\Delta}_{Y,Z}(b_{k}^{\prime}\boxtimes c_{\ell}^{\prime})

\displaystyle=u^{\Lambda,\Delta}_{Y,Z}\sum b_{i}\underbrace{\langle b_{i}|b_{k}^{\prime}\rangle_{\mathfrak{X}}}_{\in{\mathfrak{X}}(\Lambda)}\boxtimes c_{j}\underbrace{\langle c_{j}|c_{\ell}^{\prime}\rangle_{\mathfrak{X}}}_{\in{\mathfrak{X}}(\Delta)}

\displaystyle=u^{\Lambda,\Delta}_{Y,Z}\sum b_{i}\boxtimes\langle b_{i}|b_{k}^{\prime}\rangle_{\mathfrak{X}}c_{j}\langle c_{j}|c_{\ell}^{\prime}\rangle_{\mathfrak{X}}

\displaystyle=u^{\Lambda,\Delta}_{Y,Z}\sum b_{i}\boxtimes c_{j}\langle b_{i}|b_{k}^{\prime}\rangle_{\mathfrak{X}}\langle c_{j}|c_{\ell}^{\prime}\rangle_{\mathfrak{X}}

\displaystyle=\sum c_{j}\boxtimes b_{i}\langle b_{i}|b_{k}^{\prime}\rangle_{\mathfrak{X}}\langle c_{j}|c_{\ell}^{\prime}\rangle_{\mathfrak{X}}

\displaystyle=\sum c_{j}\boxtimes b_{k}^{\prime}\langle c_{j}|c_{\ell}^{\prime}\rangle_{\mathfrak{X}}

\displaystyle=\sum c_{j}\boxtimes\langle c_{j}|c_{\ell}^{\prime}\rangle_{\mathfrak{X}}b_{k}^{\prime}

\displaystyle=\sum c_{j}\langle c_{j}|c_{\ell}^{\prime}\rangle_{\mathfrak{X}}\boxtimes b_{k}^{\prime}

\displaystyle=c_{\ell}^{\prime}\boxtimes b_{k}^{\prime}.

Hence the map
u^{\Lambda,\Delta}_{Y,Z}
is a well-defined
{\mathfrak{X}}-{\mathfrak{X}}
bimodule intertwiner.
One can similarly mimic the remainder of the proofs from
[
Jon24
]
to see we have a well-defined unitary braiding.

Theorem 4.21
.

The boundary DHR bimodules
\mathsf{DHR}^{\partial}({\mathfrak{X}})
is equivalent as a unitary braided tensor category to the enriched center
Z^{\mathcal{A}}({\mathcal{X}})
.

Proof.

It remains to show that the functor
Y:Z^{\mathcal{A}}({\mathcal{X}})\to\mathsf{DHR}^{\partial}({\mathfrak{X}})
is braided.
This follows similarly to the proof of
[
Jon24
, Lem. 4.18]
based on
[
CJP24
, Prop. 6.15]
, adding the
{\mathcal{A}}
-enrichment.
For an easy way to see this, we provide a 2D graphical version of the the proof from
[
Jon24
, Lem. 4.18]
for the case
{\mathcal{A}}=\mathsf{Hilb}
, from which our result follows by adding
A
-strands going ‘back into the page,’ making the diagrams 3D.

Since the underlying object of
z\in Z({\mathcal{X}})
is a direct sum of simples in
{\mathcal{X}}
,
z
is completely determined by

{\mathcal{X}}(X\to F(z))\cong Z({\mathcal{X}})(\Tr(X)\to z)

by the Yoneda Lemma.

and observe that
\{b_{j}\}
gives a projective basis for the DHR bimodule
Y^{z}
localized at any single site
n\in{\mathbb{Z}}
that we choose.
Now choose another
w\in Z({\mathcal{X}})
with partition of unity
1_{X\otimes w}=\sum a_{i}a_{i}^{\dagger}
similar to (
4.22
),
and we obtain a projective basis
\{a_{i}\}
for
Y^{w}
localized at any other site we choose, say any
k<n
.
Observe that
\{a_{i}\boxtimes b_{j}\}
is a projective basis for
Y^{w}\boxtimes_{{\mathfrak{X}}}Y^{z}
, but it is now localized in the interval
[k,n]
.
We can now compute that our functor
Y:Z({\mathcal{X}})\to\mathsf{DHR}^{\partial}({\mathfrak{X}})
is braided.
Indeed, postcomposing with the braiding
w\otimes z\to z\otimes w
, we have

Since both
Y(\beta_{w,z})
and
u^{k,n}_{Y^{w},Y^{z}}
are
{\mathfrak{X}}-{\mathfrak{X}}
bimodular, the result follows.

When
{\mathcal{A}}
is an arbitrary braided UFC and
{\mathcal{X}}
is an arbitrary
{\mathcal{A}}
-enriched UFC, we still have projective bases for
Y^{w},Y^{z}
localized at a single boundary site as in (
4.22
).
Again using the convention from
[
GHK+24
, Rem. 2.12]
in which the strands for
w,z\in Z^{\mathcal{A}}({\mathcal{X}})
are drawn on the other side of
{\mathcal{X}}
, we see that the red
A
-strands going ‘back into the page’ play no role in the above argument.

5.
Boundary algebras of Walker-Wang models

In this section, we prove that the unitary tensor category version
[
HBJP23
,
GHK+24
]
of the Walker-Wang string net model
[
WW12
]
for a unitary braided fusion category (UBFC)
{\mathcal{A}}

(as opposed to the 6j-symbol model)
has a net of projections

p_{\Lambda}:=\prod_{p\subset\Lambda}B_{p}\prod_{\ell\subset\Lambda}A_{\ell}

satisfying the LTO axioms from
[
JNPW23
]
(see §
2.1
above for the main definitions).
We then identify the boundary algebra as a 2D braided categorical net, and we use the DHR bimodules for this net to calculate the point-like excitations.
Finally, we consider a topological boundary coming from an
{\mathcal{A}}
-enriched UFC
{\mathcal{X}}
and study the boundary LTO and its boundary DHR bimodules.

5.1.
The Walker-Wang model

Let
{\mathcal{A}}
denote a UBFC.
For simplicity we will only consider the model on a cubic lattice in three dimensions.
Schematically, the Hilbert space can be visualized as on the left hand side below, where the red edges carry labels from
\Irr({\mathcal{A}})
.
Given an
{\mathcal{A}}
-enriched UFC
{\mathcal{X}}
, we also get a 2D topological
{\mathcal{X}}
-boundary for the 3D Walker-Wang model for
{\mathcal{A}}
, pictured on the right hand side below.

or

Here, we read from bottom left to top right.

{\mathcal{L}}

{\mathcal{X}}

In the middle picture above, one uses
\Phi:{\mathcal{A}}\to{\mathcal{X}}
to resolve the plaquette operator into the vertices which meet the black
{\mathcal{X}}
edges.
There is a similar formula for the matrix coefficients
C(\xi,\xi^{\prime})
for the
B_{p}
which can be obtained by modifying
[
GHK+24
, Prop. 3.2]
which shows that the
B_{p}
are self-adjoint projectors.
There are no terms for cubes in the lattice.

As before, we define

p^{A}_{\Lambda}:=\prod_{\ell\subset\Lambda}A_{\ell}
,

p^{B}_{\Lambda}:=\prod_{p\subset\ell}B_{p}
, and
p_{\Lambda}:=p^{A}_{\Lambda}p^{B}_{\Lambda}
.
We have the following theorem for the operator
p^{B}_{\Lambda}
on
\im(p^{A}_{\Lambda})=p^{A}_{\Lambda}\bigotimes_{v\in\Lambda}{\mathcal{H}}_{v}

(again replacing
{\mathcal{H}}_{v}
for
{\mathcal{K}}_{v}
in the presence of a topological
{\mathcal{X}}
boundary.)

Lemma 5.3

(
[
GHK+24
, Thm. 3.4]
)
.

For a rectangle
\Lambda
, on
\im(p^{A}_{\Lambda})
,

p^{B}_{\Lambda}=D_{{\mathcal{A}}}^{-\#p\subset\Lambda^{\circ}+\#c\subset\Lambda^{\circ}}D_{{\mathcal{X}}}^{-\#p\subset\partial\Lambda}\cdot\eval^{\dagger}\circ\eval,

where

\Lambda^{\circ}
is the part of
\Lambda
which does not touch the
{\mathcal{X}}
boundary,

\#p\subset\Lambda^{\circ}
is the number of plaquettes in
\Lambda^{\circ}
and
\#c\subset\Lambda^{\circ}
is the number of cubes in
\Lambda
, including plaquettes and cubes which meet but are not strictly contained in
\partial\Lambda
, and
\#p\subset\partial\Lambda
is the number of plaquettes contained where
\Lambda
intersects the
{\mathcal{X}}
boundary.
Hence
\im(p_{\Lambda})
is unitarily isomorphic to the enriched skein module via an appropriately scaled evaluation map.

Definition 5.4
.

We now cut our 3D region along a vertical 2D hyperplane
{\mathcal{K}}
as follows:

(5.5)

or

We choose a distinguished half-space
{\mathbb{H}}
bounded by
{\mathcal{K}}
, which is assumed to be to the
right
of the slice in (
5.5
) above.
For a 3D rectangle
\Lambda\subset{\mathbb{H}}
, we let
I=I(\Lambda)
be the intersection
\partial\Lambda\cap{\mathcal{K}}
.
Observe that
I=\emptyset
if
\Lambda\cap{\mathcal{K}}=\emptyset
.
The tangent vectors on points of
I
are oriented according to (
5.1
), projected into the 2D plane as in the diagram in the left hand side there.
In (
5.5
) above,
I
is
the rectangle where the red lattice lines intersect the blue slice, so points in
I
are oriented from
left-to-right
.

When
I\neq\emptyset
, we define

{\mathfrak{F}}(I):=\End_{\mathcal{A}}(A^{\otimes I})

where
A^{\otimes I}
is the tensor product of the
generator
A:=\bigoplus_{a\in\Irr({\mathcal{A}})}a
over the sites in
I
.
In the presence of the
{\mathcal{X}}
topological boundary located on sites in the boundary
\partial{\mathcal{L}}
of our lattice
{\mathcal{L}}
, we modify the above definition to account for sites in
I
which meet
\partial{\mathcal{L}}
:

{\mathfrak{G}}(I):=\begin{cases}\End_{\mathcal{A}}(A^{\otimes I})&\text{if }I\cap\partial{\mathcal{L}}=\emptyset\\
\End_{\mathcal{X}}(X^{\otimes I\cap\partial{\mathcal{L}}}\lhd A^{\otimes I\setminus\partial{\mathcal{L}}})&\text{if }I\cap\partial{\mathcal{L}}\neq\emptyset\end{cases}

where
X=\bigoplus_{x\in\Irr({\mathcal{X}})}x
is our strong tensor generator of
{\mathcal{X}}
.

Just as
[
JNPW23
, Def. 4.6]
, for
\psi\in{\mathfrak{F}}(I)
, we can define a gluing operator
\Gamma_{\psi}
acting on
\bigotimes_{v\in\Lambda}{\mathcal{H}}_{v}
.
When
I
is as in (
5.5
) and

\psi\in{\mathcal{A}}(\bigotimes_{I}a_{i}\to\bigotimes_{I}b_{i})
,
\Gamma_{\psi}
first applies the projector
p_{\Lambda}
so that the edge labels of the vectors match and plaquettes are effectively filled.
This allows us to view a vector in
p_{\Lambda}\bigotimes_{v\in\Lambda}{\mathcal{H}}_{v}

as an element of the enriched skein module
[
GHK+24
, §3.1]
for
{\mathcal{A}}
, giving an element in
{\mathcal{A}}(1_{\mathcal{A}}\to A^{\otimes\partial\Lambda})
.
We can then take our desired morphism
\psi
and glue it on, first projecting to make sure the labels
a_{i}
in
\bigotimes_{I}a_{i}
match in order so composition is well-defined.
We have a similar definition for
\Gamma_{\psi}
in the presence of the
{\mathcal{X}}
toplogical boundary for
\psi\in{\mathfrak{G}}(I)
.
We must also multiply by ratios of fourth roots of quantum dimensions in order to make this a
*
-action, which are omitted in the cartoons below.

This new morphism must be resolved into a vector in
\bigotimes_{v\in\Lambda}{\mathcal{H}}_{v}
in the usual way using semisimplicity.

Arguing as in
[
JNPW23
, Lem. 4.7 and Thm. 4.8]
, but using a variant of the
sphere algebra
of
{\mathcal{A}}

[
GHK+24
, Def. 3.12]
instead of the tube algebra, we get the following theorem.

Theorem 5.6
.

The Walker-Wang model for
{\mathcal{A}}
satisfies
(LTO1)
–
(LTO4)
for
s=1
,
and the boundary algebra

{\mathfrak{B}}(\Lambda\Subset\Delta)=\left\{\Gamma_{\psi}\middle|\psi\in\End_{\mathcal{A}}(A^{\otimes I})\right\}\cong{\mathfrak{F}}(I)\qquad\qquad\qquad I=\partial\Lambda\cap\partial\Delta\cap{\mathcal{K}}.

Using a variant of the
dome algebra
of the
{\mathcal{A}}
-enriched UFC
{\mathcal{X}}

[
GHK+24
, Def. 3.6]
, we get the following theorem.

Theorem 5.7
.

The boundary Walker-Wang model for the
{\mathcal{A}}
-enriched UFC
{\mathcal{X}}
satisfies
(

∂

LTO1)
–
(

∂

LTO4)
for
s=1
, and the boundary algebra

{\mathfrak{B}}(\Lambda\Subset^{\delta}\Delta)=\left\{\Gamma_{\psi}\middle|\psi\in\End_{\mathcal{X}}(X^{\otimes I\cap\partial{\mathcal{L}}}\lhd A^{\otimes I\setminus\partial{\mathcal{L}}}))\right\}\cong{\mathfrak{G}}(I)\qquad\qquad I=\partial\Lambda\cap\partial\Delta\cap{\mathcal{K}}.

5.2.
DHR bimodules for the Walker-Wang model

In order to compute the the DHR bimodules for the boundary algebra of the Walker-Wang model for
{\mathcal{A}}
, we first analyze the boundary DHR bimodules for the boundary Walker-Wang model for the
{\mathcal{A}}
-enriched UFC
{\mathcal{X}}
.
We saw in Theorem
5.7
above that the boundary algebra for this boundary LTO is given by the braided categorical net with boundary
{\mathfrak{G}}
associated to the
{\mathcal{A}}
-enriched UFC
{\mathcal{X}}
.
In Theorem
4.21
above, we showed that
\mathsf{DHR}^{\partial}({\mathfrak{G}})\cong Z^{\mathcal{A}}({\mathcal{X}})
, the enriched center of
{\mathcal{X}}
, a.k.a., the Müger centralizer
{\mathcal{A}}^{\prime}\subset Z({\mathcal{X}})
.

With this theorem in hand, we can now compute the DHR bimodules for the boundary algebra
{\mathfrak{B}}\cong{\mathfrak{F}}
of the
{\mathcal{A}}
Walker-Wang model.
We apply a 3D folding trick along our cut
{\mathcal{K}}
to view the underlying UFC of
{\mathcal{A}}
as an
{\mathcal{A}}^{\rm rev}\boxtimes{\mathcal{A}}
-enriched UFC.
Folding effectively doubles each lattice site away from
{\mathcal{K}}
and views sites in
{\mathcal{K}}
as the boundary
\partial{\mathcal{L}}
of the lattice.
We observe now that a DHR bimodule localized in a rectangle
I\subset{\mathcal{K}}
can be viewed as a boundary DHR bimodule localized in
I
, as
I
is now constrained to the boundary
\partial{\mathcal{L}}={\mathcal{K}}
.
By Theorem
4.21
, we have
\mathsf{DHR}^{\partial}({\mathfrak{B}})\cong Z^{{\mathcal{A}}^{\rm rev}\boxtimes{\mathcal{A}}}({\mathcal{A}})\cong Z_{2}({\mathcal{A}})
, the
Müger center
of
{\mathcal{A}}
, as UBFCs
[
Müg03
]
.
Unfolding, we see that indeed
\mathsf{DHR}({\mathfrak{B}})\cong Z_{2}({\mathcal{A}})
as UBFCs, as the definition for the braiding on
\mathsf{DHR}({\mathfrak{B}})
can without loss of generality be defined in terms of rectangles localized along our cut
{\mathcal{K}}
.

Appendix A
AF actions of unitary multifusion categories

In this section, we review how one can get an AF action of a unitary multifusion category on an AF
{\mathrm{C}}^{*}
-algebra by adapting the results of
[
BCE+25
]
.
We begin by reviewing these results.

Let
{\mathcal{C}}
be a unitary multifusion category.
Fix a
faithful 2-shading
on
{\mathcal{C}}
, i.e., a decomposition
1_{\mathcal{C}}=1_{+}\oplus 1_{-}
such that
{\mathcal{C}}_{+-}:=1_{+}\otimes{\mathcal{C}}\otimes 1_{-}\neq 0
.
Observe that the similarly defined
{\mathcal{C}}_{++},{\mathcal{C}}_{-+},{\mathcal{C}}_{--}
are all nonzero, and we may think of
{\mathcal{C}}
as a
2\times 2
block of categories

{\mathcal{C}}=\begin{pmatrix}{\mathcal{C}}_{++}&{\mathcal{C}}_{+-}\\
{\mathcal{C}}_{-+}&{\mathcal{C}}_{--}\end{pmatrix}.

We represent
1_{+}
by an unshaded region and
1_{-}
by a shaded region.
Pick a generator
X\in{\mathcal{C}}_{+-}
(which generates
{\mathcal{C}}
under tensor product
\otimes
, algebraic duals
\vee
, direct sum
\oplus
, and idempotent completion), and we equip
{\mathcal{C}}
with the
standard unitary dual functor

\vee
with respect to
X

[
Pen20
]
such that the loop parameters for
X
are scalars:

\psi(\id_{1_{+}})=\psi(\id_{1_{-}})=1
.
This means that
\Tr^{\mathcal{C}}:=\psi\circ\tr_{L}^{\vee}=\psi\circ\tr_{R}^{\vee}
is a unitary trace on
{\mathcal{C}}
which equips it with the structure of a
2-Hilbert space
in the sense of
[
Bae97
]
.
Each hom space
{\mathcal{C}}(a\to b)
is equipped with a Hilbert space structure given by

\langle f|g\rangle_{a\to b}:=\Tr^{\mathcal{C}}_{a}(f^{\dagger}\circ g)=\Tr^{\mathcal{C}}_{b}(g\circ f^{\dagger})

which satisfies that for all
f:a\to b
,
g:b\to c
, and
h:a\to c
,

\langle g|h\circ f^{\dagger}\rangle_{b\to c}=\langle g\circ f|h\rangle_{a\to c}=\langle f|g^{\dagger}\circ h\rangle_{a\to b}.

Construction A.2
.

One now constructs two AF
{\mathrm{C}}^{*}
-algebras as follows.
First, we write

X^{\alt\otimes n}:=\underbrace{X\otimes X^{\vee}\otimes X\otimes\cdots X^{?}}_{n\text{ tensorands}}\qquad\qquad\text{and}\qquad\qquad(X^{\vee})^{\alt\otimes n}:=\underbrace{X^{\vee}\otimes X\otimes X^{\vee}\otimes\cdots X^{?}}_{n\text{ tensorands}}

where the question marks are determined by parity of
n
.
We define

A_{n}:=\End_{\mathcal{C}}(X^{\alt\otimes n})\qquad\qquad\text{and}\qquad\qquad B_{n}:=\End_{\mathcal{C}}((X^{\vee})^{\alt\otimes n}).

We have the inductive limit AF algebras
A:=\varinjlim A_{n}
and
B:=\varinjlim B_{n}
,
where the inclusions are always given by tensoring by identities on the right, i.e., taking inductive limit over the map

Here, a strand labeled
n
denotes
X^{\alt\otimes n}
or
(X^{\vee})^{\alt\otimes n}
,
and the single strand represents either
X
or
X^{\vee}
depending on the parity of
n
.
The top string is always
X
for
A
and
X^{\vee}
for
B
.
As the map (
A.1
) is an isomorphism, we see that

Z(A)\cong\End_{\mathcal{C}}(1_{+})
and
Z(B)\cong\End_{\mathcal{C}}(1_{-})
.
This also relies on the fact that eventually the Bratteli diagrams for
A,B
are stationary
[
GdlHJ89
, Thm. 4.1.4]
(see also
[
CHPS21
, §3.1]
).
The inclusion
A\subset B
is obtained by taking the inductive limit of the map
\id_{X^{\vee}}\otimes-:A_{n}\hookrightarrow B_{n+1}
given by

Now on
A_{n}
, we can define a faithful tracial state by
\tr_{n}:=d_{X}^{-n}\Tr^{\mathcal{C}}
, and similarly for
B_{n}
.
(The normalization for
\psi
ensures that
\tr_{n}(1)=1
for all
n
for both
A
and
B
.)
Note that the inclusions

A_{n}\hookrightarrow A_{n+1}

and

A_{n}\hookrightarrow B_{n+1}

are both trace preserving.
We can thus complete
A,B
to
\rm II_{1}

multifactors
(direct sums of
\rm II_{1}
factors)
{\mathcal{A}},{\mathcal{B}}
by using the GNS construction with respect to
\tr:=\varinjlim\tr_{n}
,
which yields a homogeneous connected finite index inclusion whose standard invariant
({\mathcal{C}}({\mathcal{A}}\subset{\mathcal{B}}),{}_{\mathcal{A}}L^{2}{\mathcal{B}}_{\mathcal{B}})
is unitarily equivalent to
({\mathcal{C}},X)

[
BCE+25
, Prop. 6.5]
.
These results rely on Popa’s generating tunnel for finite depth inclusions
[
Pop90
]

and the Ocneanu Compactness Theorem
[
JS97
]
,
[
EK98
, §11.4]
, generalized to the multifactor setting
[
BCE+25
, Appendices B and C]
.
To see this, one performs Jones’ basic construction to get a tower of multifactors equipped with traces

{\mathcal{A}}_{0}:={\mathcal{A}}\subset{\mathcal{B}}:={\mathcal{A}}_{1}\overset{e_{1}}{\subset}{\mathcal{A}}_{2}\overset{e_{2}}{\subset}{\mathcal{A}}_{3}\subset\cdots

and the
higher relative commutants
can be identified with endomorphism spaces in
{\mathcal{C}}
as follows
[
Bis97
]
:

(A.3)

\displaystyle{\mathcal{A}}_{0}^{\prime}\cap{\mathcal{A}}_{2k}

\displaystyle\cong\End_{{\mathcal{A}}-{\mathcal{A}}}(L^{2}{\mathcal{B}}^{\boxtimes_{\mathcal{A}}k})\cong\End_{\mathcal{C}}((X\otimes X^{\vee})^{\otimes k})

\displaystyle{\mathcal{A}}_{0}^{\prime}\cap{\mathcal{A}}_{2k+1}

\displaystyle\cong\End_{{\mathcal{A}}-{\mathcal{B}}}(L^{2}{\mathcal{B}}^{\boxtimes_{\mathcal{A}}k+1})\cong\End_{\mathcal{C}}((X\otimes X^{\vee})^{\otimes k}\otimes X)

\displaystyle{\mathcal{A}}_{1}^{\prime}\cap{\mathcal{A}}_{2k+1}

\displaystyle\cong\End_{{\mathcal{B}}-{\mathcal{B}}}(L^{2}{\mathcal{B}}^{\boxtimes_{\mathcal{A}}k})\cong\End_{\mathcal{C}}((X^{\vee}\otimes X)^{\otimes k+1})

\displaystyle{\mathcal{A}}_{1}^{\prime}\cap{\mathcal{A}}_{2k+2}

\displaystyle\cong\End_{{\mathcal{B}}-{\mathcal{A}}}(L^{2}{\mathcal{B}}^{\boxtimes_{\mathcal{A}}k+1})\cong\End_{\mathcal{C}}((X^{\vee}\otimes X)^{\otimes k}\otimes X^{\vee}).

We thus get a unitary tensor functor into
\mathsf{Bim}({\mathcal{A}}\oplus{\mathcal{B}})
from the full subcategory
{\mathcal{C}}_{0}\subset{\mathcal{C}}
whose objects are of the form
X^{\alt\otimes n}
and
(X^{\vee})^{\alt\otimes n}
.
We then use the universal property of unitary idempotent completion to uniquely extend the functor to

{\mathcal{F}}:{\mathcal{C}}=\begin{pmatrix}{\mathcal{C}}_{++}&{\mathcal{C}}_{+-}\\
{\mathcal{C}}_{-+}&{\mathcal{C}}_{--}\end{pmatrix}\hookrightarrow\begin{pmatrix}\mathsf{Bim}({\mathcal{A}})&\mathsf{Bim}({\mathcal{A}},{\mathcal{B}})\\
\mathsf{Bim}({\mathcal{B}},{\mathcal{A}})&\mathsf{Bim}({\mathcal{B}})\end{pmatrix}=\mathsf{Bim}({\mathcal{A}}\oplus{\mathcal{B}}).

There are also uniqueness results in
[
BCE+25
]
, but these are not necessary for the results in this article.

Example A.4
.

multistep basic construction
.

.

We simply observe that the
{\mathcal{A}}
-valued inner product on
F(c)_{n}
coming from the trace on
{\mathcal{A}}
lands in
A_{n}
and is given by

\langle\eta|\xi\rangle_{A_{n}}:=\eta^{\dagger}\circ\xi\in\End((A_{n})_{A_{n}})=A_{n}.

Moreover, the inclusions
-\otimes\id:F(c)_{n}\hookrightarrow F(c)_{n+1}

are compatible with the inclusions
-\otimes\id:A_{n}\hookrightarrow A_{n+1}
, and

\langle\eta\otimes\id|\xi\otimes\id\rangle_{A_{n+1}}=(\eta\otimes\id)^{\dagger}\circ(\xi\otimes\id)=(\eta^{\dagger}\circ\xi)\otimes\id=\langle\eta|\xi\rangle_{A_{n}}\otimes\id.

Finally, this map is compatible with the associator and unitors in
{\mathcal{C}}_{++}
, yielding a tensorator for our fully faithful tensor functor
{\mathcal{F}}:{\mathcal{C}}_{++}\to\mathsf{Bim}({\mathcal{A}})
.

Remark A.5
.

One does not need to pass to the von Neumann algebraic closures in order for the results on standard invariants and unitary tensor functors to hold.
Indeed, these results hold on the level of the AF
{\mathrm{C}}^{*}
-algebras and their Hilbert
{\mathrm{C}}^{*}
-bimodules/correspondences.
The standard invariant for
A\subset B
where again the inclusion is tensor product on the left with
\id_{X^{\vee}}
, and again, we have a unitary equivalence
({\mathcal{C}}(A\subset B),{}_{A}B_{B})\cong({\mathcal{C}},X)
.
One argues this by showing we have canonical inclusions

\displaystyle\End_{\mathcal{C}}((X{\otimes}X^{\vee})^{{\otimes}n})

\displaystyle\subseteq

\displaystyle\End_{A-A}(B^{\boxtimes_{A}n})

\displaystyle\subseteq

\displaystyle\End_{{\mathcal{A}}-{\mathcal{A}}}(L^{2}{\mathcal{B}}^{\boxtimes_{A}n})

\displaystyle\cong

\displaystyle\End_{\mathcal{C}}((X{\otimes}X^{\vee})^{{\otimes}n})

\displaystyle\End_{\mathcal{C}}((X{\otimes}X^{\vee})^{{\otimes}n}{\otimes}X)

\displaystyle\subseteq

\displaystyle\End_{A-B}(B^{\boxtimes_{A}n+1})

\displaystyle\subseteq

\displaystyle\End_{{\mathcal{A}}-{\mathcal{B}}}(L^{2}{\mathcal{B}}^{\boxtimes_{A}n+1})

\displaystyle\cong

\displaystyle\End_{\mathcal{C}}((X{\otimes}X^{\vee})^{{\otimes}n}{\otimes}X)

\displaystyle\End_{\mathcal{C}}((X^{\vee}{\otimes}X)^{{\otimes}n})

\displaystyle\subseteq

\displaystyle\End_{B-B}(B^{\boxtimes_{A}n+1})

\displaystyle\subseteq

\displaystyle\End_{{\mathcal{B}}-{\mathcal{B}}}(L^{2}{\mathcal{B}}^{\boxtimes_{A}n+1})

\displaystyle\cong

\displaystyle\End_{\mathcal{C}}((X^{\vee}{\otimes}X)^{{\otimes}n})

\displaystyle\End_{\mathcal{C}}((X^{\vee}{\otimes}X)^{{\otimes}n}{\otimes}X^{\vee})

\displaystyle\subseteq

\displaystyle\End_{B-A}(B^{\boxtimes_{A}n+1})

\displaystyle\subseteq

\displaystyle\End_{{\mathcal{B}}-{\mathcal{A}}}(L^{2}{\mathcal{B}}^{\boxtimes_{A}n+1})

\displaystyle\cong

\displaystyle\End_{\mathcal{C}}((X^{\vee}{\otimes}X)^{{\otimes}n}{\otimes}X^{\vee})

which are thus isomorphisms by the finite dimensionality of endomorphism spaces of
{\mathcal{C}}
.
We thus obtain a fully faithful unitary tensor functor

F:{\mathcal{C}}=\begin{pmatrix}{\mathcal{C}}_{++}&{\mathcal{C}}_{+-}\\
{\mathcal{C}}_{-+}&{\mathcal{C}}_{--}\end{pmatrix}\hookrightarrow\begin{pmatrix}\mathsf{Bim}(A)&\mathsf{Bim}(A,B)\\
\mathsf{Bim}(B,A)&\mathsf{Bim}(B)\end{pmatrix}=\mathsf{Bim}(A\oplus B).

such that
X\mapsto{}_{A}B_{B}
.
Similar to before, each
F(c):=\varinjlim F(c)_{n}
now taken with respect to the
A
-valued inner product
\varinjlim\langle\,\cdot\,|\,\cdot\,\rangle_{A_{n}}
gives an explicit description of an
inductive limit
A-A

{\mathrm{C}}^{*}
-Hilbert bimodule.

Example A.6
.

Let
{\mathcal{C}}
be a unitary multifusion category, and let
{\mathcal{M}}_{\mathcal{C}}
be a unitary right
{\mathcal{C}}
-module category.
For any choice of generator
W\in{\mathcal{M}}
, we can run the above construction to obtain a fully faithful unitary tensor functor

{\mathcal{E}}=\begin{pmatrix}\End({\mathcal{M}}_{\mathcal{C}})&{\mathcal{M}}\\
{\mathcal{M}}^{\rm op}&{\mathcal{C}}\end{pmatrix}\hookrightarrow\begin{pmatrix}\mathsf{Bim}(A)&\mathsf{Bim}(A,B)\\
\mathsf{Bim}(B,A)&\mathsf{Bim}(B)\end{pmatrix}=\mathsf{Bim}(A\oplus B)

such that
W\mapsto{}_{A}B_{B}
.

We now turn to the explicit example that appears in §
3.2
above, and we describe how to employ the results of
[
BCE+25
]
described above in order to prove the corresponding construction is fully faithful.

Example A.7
.

Suppose now that we want to work with two generators: some
W\in{\mathcal{M}}
and
X\in{\mathcal{C}}
rather than a single generator.
We impose the requirement that
X\in{\mathcal{C}}
is a strong tensor generator, i.e., there is an
n\in{\mathbb{N}}
such that every
c\in\Irr({\mathcal{C}})
appears as a summand of
X^{\otimes n}
.

First, we use the above construction for our generator
X\in{\mathcal{C}}
to obtain a fully faithful unitary tensor functor
{\mathcal{C}}\to\mathsf{Bim}(A)
.
(We do this by first replacing
{\mathcal{C}}
with
\operatorname{Mat}_{2}({\mathcal{C}})
and viewing our generator
X
as living off the diagonal.)

We now employ the
Q-system completion
technique from
[
CHPJP22
]
.
The basic idea is that given a fully faithful tensor functor
F:{\mathcal{C}}\to\mathsf{Bim}(A)
for a
{\mathrm{C}}^{*}
-algebra
A
and a Q-system (
{\mathrm{C}}^{*}
Frobenius algebra object)
Q\in{\mathcal{C}}
, one can form the
Q-system realization

|Q|_{F}
, which is the
{\mathrm{C}}^{*}
-algebra
F(Q)\in\mathsf{Bim}(A)
, equipped with its own multiplication and involution.
There are many utilities for
|Q|_{F}
; the one we are most interested in is
[
CHPJP22
, Cor. C]
, which states that we have a fully faithful composite 2-functor

\mathsf{QSys}({\mathcal{C}})\xrightarrow{\mathsf{QSys}(F)}\mathsf{QSys}(\mathsf{Bim}(A))\xrightarrow{|\cdot|}\mathsf{C^{*}Alg}.

As a corollary, for any Q-system
Q\in{\mathcal{C}}
, we get a fully faithful unitary tensor functor from the unitary (multi)tensor category
{}_{Q}{\mathcal{C}}_{Q}
into
\mathsf{Bim}(|Q|_{F})
.

There is still one technical subtlety to overcome to deal with our specific example.
Given our module generator
W\in{\mathcal{M}}
, we would like that the inductive limit algebra

B:=\varinjlim\End_{\mathcal{M}}(W\lhd X^{\otimes n})

is the Q-system realization of
\underline{\End}_{\mathcal{M}}(W)\in{\mathcal{C}}
.
In more detail, one uses duality in
{\mathcal{E}}
so that

B:=\varinjlim\Hom_{\mathcal{C}}(X^{\otimes n}\to W^{\vee}\otimes W\otimes X^{\otimes n})

where multiplication is given by

The main problem here is that the choice of cap above depends on a choice of unitary duality for
{\mathcal{E}}
.
Moreover, one must use the notion of
unitary internal end
in order for
\underline{\End}_{\mathcal{M}}(W)
to define an honest element of
{\mathcal{C}}
and not just the underlying multifusion category
{\mathcal{C}}^{\natural}
where we have forgotten the dagger structure.
Both of these goals can be accomplished by endowing
{\mathcal{M}}
with a carefully chosen
unitary module trace
as in §
3
, which allows one to use
unitary adjunction

[
HPT24
, §2.1]
to constuct the unitary itnernal hom as in
[
CFH+24
, §3.3]
.
Indeed, when
{\mathcal{M}}
is indecomposable,
\End({\mathcal{M}}_{\mathcal{C}})
is fusion, so the bubble for
W
is always a positive scalar.
There is thus a unique unitary module trace such that the
W
-bubble is equal to one.
6
6

6

This is entirely analogous to the situation of an operator
T:H\to K
such that
T^{*}T=r1_{H}
for some
r>0
.
We can uniquely rescale the inner product on
H
so that
T
becomes unitary.

For an arbitrary module, there is a unique faithful convex combination of traces on the indecomposable summands so that the bubble for
W
in
\End({\mathcal{M}}_{\mathcal{C}})
equals one.
This immediately implies that
|\underline{\End}_{\mathcal{C}}(W)|
is a (special) Q-system

Now by
[
CHPJP22
, Cor. C]
, we have a fully faithful tensor functor
\End({\mathcal{M}}_{\mathcal{C}})\hookrightarrow\mathsf{Bim}(B)
.
Unpacking as in Example
A.4
above,
for
F\in\End({\mathcal{M}}_{\mathcal{C}})
,
we obtain exactly the DHR bimodules
Y^{F}:=\varinjlim Y^{F}_{n}
where

Y^{F}_{n}:={\mathcal{M}}(W\lhd X^{\otimes n}\to FW\lhd\otimes X^{\otimes n})

for the boundary algebra
{\mathfrak{B}}=B=\varinjlim\End_{\mathcal{M}}(W\lhd X^{\otimes n})
from §
3.2
above.

One can also repeat the above analysis for the Q-system
1\oplus|\underline{\End}_{\mathcal{C}}(W)|\in{\mathcal{C}}
in order to obtain a fully faithful tensor functor

{\mathcal{E}}=\begin{pmatrix}\End({\mathcal{M}}_{\mathcal{C}})&{\mathcal{M}}\\
{\mathcal{M}}^{\rm op}&{\mathcal{C}}\end{pmatrix}\hookrightarrow\begin{pmatrix}\mathsf{Bim}(B)&\mathsf{Bim}(B,A)\\
\mathsf{Bim}(A,B)&\mathsf{Bim}(A)\end{pmatrix}=\mathsf{Bim}(B\oplus A).
